subject: I just finished a long day of knocking on doors

body:
Our end-of-month deadline is just hours away.
Hi Peter, it's Pramila.
I just finished a long day of knocking on doors here in Seattle! I am so inspired by all the volunteers who turned out to help support not only my campaign, but progressive candidates up and down the ballot.
But we won't let up until the polls close. This election is too important to leave to chance, and I'm counting on you to help us cross the finish line.
With our end-of-month deadline just hours away, will you chip in at the link below to help us fund our final efforts to get out the vote?
[**https://secure.actblue.com/donate/pj-em-20261031-2**](https://act.pramilaforcongress.com/go/47393?c0=pj-em-20261031-2.PCLBQn&refcode=em20261031-6908&t=1&akid=6908%2E420207%2EO9t3kc)
Thank you, thank you, thank you for your support.
— PJ

It's the last night of October and just hours from our end of month deadline.
I'm the only Democratic Senator up for reelection in a state Trump won in 2024. And MAGA has spent tens of millions to flip this seat.
Before you turn in: **[Can you rush $10 before midnight to help me win in Georgia?](https://substack.com/redirect/e9d92f9a-4bab-48c0-bfc0-701209184b31?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**

When I first ran for Senate six years ago, it was because I believed the election of someone so deeply unfit for the presidency posed a danger to the country.
Many people said it couldn't be done. But you believed -- not just in me, but in the idea that Georgia could lead, and that our Republic is worth defending.
Then we won. Not just a Senate seat, but the Senate majority for Democrats.
Now Trump has launched a power grab unprecedented in our history, abusing his power and trying to poison our Republic with fear and intimidation.
Americans are now living in fear of their own government.
I'm fighting back.
And I need you with me.

Case File No DRT-ED-AUSTIN · Special File · The Austin Lab
Apple Says American Factories Were On Track to Make More Than 19 Billion Chips for Its Products in 2025. Most iPhone Owners Have No Idea Where They Come From.
In August 2025, Apple raised its U.S. investment pledge to $600 billion and named partners building chips for the iPhone on American soil. Austin, Texas, sits close to the middle of that effort. The parts inside your phone have quietly become a national priority.
Threat level 3/5 — Guarded

Most people know who designs the iPhone. Almost nobody knows who makes the dozens of chips inside it. Those suppliers rarely make headlines, yet each one can collect a share of every phone sold. And as Washington pushes chipmaking back to America, some of them are getting a bigger role.
The evidence board
| | What We Know
---|---
| EVIDENCE
---
**Exhibit A — the pledge.** On August 6, 2025, Apple raised its U.S. commitment to $600 billion over four years and launched its American Manufacturing Program.
| EVIDENCE
---
**Exhibit B — Austin.** Apple said it’s working with Samsung at its Austin chip plant on a manufacturing technology never used before anywhere in the world, to supply chips for iPhones sold worldwide.
| EVIDENCE
---
**Exhibit C — the scale.** Apple said the U.S. silicon supply chain was on track to produce more than 19 billion chips for its products in 2025.
| EVIDENCE
---
**Exhibit D — the campus.** Apple’s second Austin campus is expanding, with three more buildings under construction, including a research lab for hardware and software teams.
| OUR THEORY
---
When the world’s most valuable phone maker moves its supply chain home, the small suppliers behind it can become much more important, and much more valuable.

Turn off the lights. Lock the doors. Check under the bed, Fellow Patriot.

Because tonight, on Halloween, something truly terrifying is creeping toward South Carolina.

It isn't a ghost. It isn't a ghoul. **It's Annie Andrews, and she's been feeding on $25 MILLION in liberal cash to grow stronger.**

In just three days, she could crawl out of the shadows and into the U.S. Senate.

And if she does, here's the horror that follows her home:

[](http://links.freedomfirstalert.com/u/click?_t=9ca143e971904d26a973d002cb0ae7f7&_m=3932ea170e87421ab7a40d9ac55d1273&_e=iOLBrK43Um7VOJiGCRBa8gvNvuXWqtBj-39C6gaBJmM4fxRlgH_oo16rsbGqdA1y9wVXl0u8hh3JELHoQucBx8gxeoFH-Qb-mu8YPDU3VMaZeJOTmX9-iBEQ2JN2ZsLwjgRcN2XwpyCFMEzRg6L14Lsg41nWQxgUPMeqP6hTAsjT2dW7SqXGgxrk4qjism0ouswBcuamQwGt5uD8CwE8aF-ds4YZL5eiHrqxCYnXKW0vJccbGrLcSIKkc88xldDrzz5Oo10_EJBe4hsjoSdTYIIs7PuDPJFw3Oicy6M7WWmgaJc1Ntwhu35fRrNXBddGlLh4PriB7Xp_CMTtroZ7KmiB_8cP2HviP1L9mLDJmmOB8W0nTurrDPGueKOgpW8KWwLIhnN4tPv1_TkHb2oYCyFBZ2XHVFX1rQ1D3H6Bnf43-jhfQqJXfeI2-yyfPgYOLFXX3Hvfz7U1QEna80A5hTAkGP7s-7KFFCuXYvc_6mG1aWtTYJDl6SsUSXxdWN0cwewdNgQTu4swU8NlulypM--M085hR2O5jsLhBWyX0ZS7Zet-fBnnp8V_yqjWODtN-gTKHBVWehClT9Mh4hyCaB5xMhW95m9vI_zfKW3sS_gPOivCO8dgWYDP7gzVd_ErcazvKl1pdzrtmiktLQUDatuZ606f5-UYv8iBgFKg7FJOgIwDa53GDB-bn_qui-iKUoX5D0L7qyYv7x6PPLbZ7mxxBR3zXnFAw7jlscibr-8%3D)
This isn't a haunted house you can walk out of. _There's no exit sign_. **If Annie Andrews wins, this nightmare lasts six long years.**

She is the most radical Democrat ever nominated statewide in South Carolina, and the Radical Left has poured $25 million into her campaign because they know exactly what she'll do with that Senate seat.

Only one person stands between South Carolina and this horror story: **Darline Graham.**

# [](https://act.wesmoore.com/go/8?t=1&akid=2234%2E1086043%2EJHAoPr)
Hi Peter, it’s Lieutenant Governor Aruna Miller.
**_Leave No One Behind._**
Those are the first words you see when you drive into Maryland, and they're the promise Wes and I made to every Marylander on day one of taking office.
Together, we've made real progress. We accelerated the path to a $15 minimum wage. We've sent more than $200 million in utility rebates to families struggling with energy costs. Violent crime is dropping, our economy is stronger, and our public schools are getting better.
But the job's not done.
**Election Day is just 2 days away, Peter.** Dan Cox and his MAGA allies are spending millions in attack ads to flip the governorship and take Maryland backward.
We can’t let that happen — and we’re counting on your support to fight back.
**[Will you chip in $5 or any amount right now to help us finish the job and keep building a Maryland that leaves no one behind?](https://act.wesmoore.com/go/417?c0=wes-em-20261101-1.7SDqKI&refcode=em-20261101-1&t=2&akid=2234%2E1086043%2EJHAoPr)**

With gratitude,
Aruna Miller

name: Kylie Glatfelter
subject: Nieshalla: Indiana’s Financial Turnaround Success Story
body:
No images? [Click here](https://indianarepublicancentralcommittee.cmail20.com/t/y-e-fhkpyk-hhlljjcji-o/)
# **Nieshalla: Indiana 's Financial Turnaround Success Story**
By Indiana State Comptroller Elise NieshallaIndiana has a financial turnaround story to remember - I dare say, on par with the remarkable transformation of Indiana University football. We've gone from headlines twenty-plus years ago like "Indiana's financial hole is staggering" by the Indiana Fiscal Policy Institute to more recent ones like "[Balanced budget amendment passes](https://indianarepublicancentralcommittee.cmail20.com/t/y-l-fhkpyk-hhlljjcji-r/)" and "[Indiana's state budget reserves jump 60% in past year to $4B](https://indianarepublicancentralcommittee.cmail20.com/t/y-l-fhkpyk-hhlljjcji-y/)."In fact, in 2002, when Democrats were at the helm, Indiana closed its books with only six cents in General Fund reserves, and our total reserve funds were spent down by 74% while hundreds of millions of dollars in payments to our schools were delayed.Just as the IU Hoosiers went from losing the most games in college football history to becoming champions, we've gone from closing our books "in the black" by six cents to having a balanced budget amendment in our Indiana Constitution that is the gold standard for the states. As I like to say, we've gone from **_six cents to common sense._** In addition, the State of Indiana has gone from being in the bottom half of the _Rich States, Poor States_ ranking by the American Legislative Exchange Council to now being in the top ten. We also have the fourth-lowest debt per capita among the states, along with growth rates for population and GDP that outpace all our neighboring states.Even the Chicago Bears have come to see Indiana as the land of milk and honey.When Governor Mitch Daniels and a Republican-led legislature came on the scene in 2004, they got to work turning our State around financially. Due to the fiscal transformation they were able to accomplish, the State of Indiana started running a clever ad campaign to lure businesses from Illinois and California to the great Hoosier State -- and the message, "Admit it, you find me fiscally attractive," was compelling then, and is even more so today.Now after two decades of Republican leadership prioritizing fiscal responsibility, discipline and transparency, Indiana's financial transformation is a true success story of a state that's been put back on financial high ground with balanced budgets, healthy reserves, low debt, well-funded pensions, and a AAA credit rating.Furthermore, the Indiana General Assembly has lowered the individual income tax rate from 3.4% to 2.95%, and it will reach a new low next year of 2.9%. All the while, our tax base and revenues have grown, giving us the ability to implement a Gas Tax Holiday when Hoosiers needed relief the most -- and still reimburse revenue to counties, cities and towns to make their transportation budgets whole. In addition, Indiana is on track to achieve fully-funded status a decade ahead of schedule for the once-struggling Pre-96 Teacher Pension Fund -- and we have paid cash for capital projects and issued two taxpayer refunds.To top it off, we are leading the way in bringing the bright light of transparency to federal dollars coming to Indiana through the newly launched Federal Funding Expenditures Dashboard or "The FEDD" -- a phenomenal new tool to help state agencies, our U.S. District Attorneys, the FBI, the DOJ, the media and public expose fraud. We are an open book, and sunlight is the best disinfectant.While we often point out how Indiana's financial health is leaps and bounds ahead of Illinois' -- our debt per capita is $169 while theirs is $2,332 -- we hope our fiscal success serves as an inspiration to them and other struggling states, like IU's football program is to other colleges across the country.It is now our responsibility to keep Indiana financially strong and stable as the bright star of the Midwest and beyond.Indiana has done the hard work to turn itself around, and may we be an inspiration to our beloved country that is facing the tremendous challenge of being $40 trillion in debt.As Hoosiers, we now also need to help build a movement to turn around our country's finances and **_Make America Like Indiana._** This election, Republicans ask for your vote to continue advancing fiscal responsibility, discipline and transparency for our great State. Let's do our utmost to keep Indiana strong. [](https://indianarepublicancentralcommittee.cmail20.com/t/y-l-fhkpyk-hhlljjcji-j/)[](https://indianarepublicancentralcommittee.cmail20.com/t/y-l-fhkpyk-hhlljjcji-t/)[](https://indianarepublicancentralcommittee.cmail20.com/t/y-l-fhkpyk-hhlljjcji-i/)[](https://indianarepublicancentralcommittee.cmail20.com/t/y-l-fhkpyk-hhlljjcji-d/)[](https://indianarepublicancentralcommittee.cmail20.com/t/y-l-fhkpyk-hhlljjcji-h/) | [Unsubscribe](https://indianarepublicancentralcommittee.cmail20.com/t/y-u-fhkpyk-hhlljjcji-b/)
---

Dear Patriot,

Right now, in campaign offices across this country, people are looking at the new volunteer a little differently, and
https://click.parlermailer.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNDcsInQiOjc2NywicyI6MTJ9AAwAAAAAA91DMWlFcs3Vm5Lq5bY20KJLTa08YUAvQ0HwScNud3NYP_Gev9XVqvynVsSNSHnCQHc4KNs8lFvuVRPUyM2R-iBhwE6zKgR_tiid9bWunA
that's exactly why I need you with me.

Two weeks ago, I posted a warning to every midterm campaign in America: “We have undercover people inside midterm campaigns across the United States.” And I told them:
“I'm watching every single thing you ALL are doing.”

714,000 people saw that post. The campaigns saw it too. Then Detroit came out, and a man who swore he could spot one of us from across the room learned that he had been talking to one of my journalists all along.

So what's on the other tapes? I can't tell you yet, and I want you to understand exactly why, because the reason is the same thing that made Detroit hold up the moment it went public.

I said in that same post that we would not release footage until we had checked the facts, corroborated our sources and gotten comment, so that every story was absolutely bulletproof. That promise is the most expensive part of what we do. It means editors reviewing every hour of raw footage, researchers checking every claim against the public record, and calls to every person on tape to give them a chance to explain. Then the lawyers read every word.
https://click.parlermailer.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNDcsInQiOjc2NywicyI6MTJ9AAwAAAAAA91DMWlGUX_9Wm4XqPtiRP1WxDMSe4VhQ3pvIKDQfeR4_PommydOVHQFTNYrsZFikr-dcHhjRsqJjBqvpCK_pWPc3vVSnTSz8f5H5ulkwQ
Help me keep that promise.

https://click.parlermailer.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNDcsInQiOjc2NywicyI6MTJ9AAwAAAAAA91DMWlHbWVNl_J-6I1ty-_M0leQrWtb6_6ls6m0qu28qLkBYHwPAwHEXa8yXbzsrQhMnDGSdR5NTnr0yMnFVnKmuVZjSdOSazSn_TUVNw

It also means I won't rush. If a story is ready before Tuesday, you'll see it. If it needs one more source, it waits. I would rather be right than first, because when the denials come, and they always come, our story has to be the one still standing.

Detroit showed what happens when we do it right: a campaign statement, a party statement and a staffer who is no longer employed. The next one will be held to the same standard.
https://click.parlermailer.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNDcsInQiOjc2NywicyI6MTJ9AAwAAAAAA91DMWlIbChhiRiMmeYjRaMh2AUfzoVmmDY5kwwpmoOfoKq1LqzOWFhGPxBsUoiEgias0EvTCNCmMVO_AczoANfWOTDRwTYR22yxEf2lAw
Help me get it out the door.

Covering the $47,000 we spent on Detroit is what lets my team stay focused on the next release instead of the last bill. We have two days left.

subject: Two days
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Small Town PAC, [smalltownpac
body:
Small Town PAC is making sure our slate has what they need to win.
#
It’s now or never, Peter.
As I write this, _Election Day is just two days away._ That leaves no room for error, but we have a plan to win on Tuesday.
Small Town PAC is backing a strong slate of nine Democratic candidates running for Congress and governor across the country. I’ve run plenty of tough races myself, and **I know there’s only one surefire way to make sure they come out on top: actually getting out and talking to voters.**
There’s nothing like a good face-to-face conversation. Not only does it give you the chance to address people’s concerns directly, but it also helps us rebuild the sense of community that’s been fractured by this divisive administration in Washington.
If our candidates like Amy Acton in Ohio and Jake Johnson in Minnesota are going to win, we have to make sure their teams reach as many voters as possible before polls close on Tuesday.
Doing that kind of voter contact the right way isn’t cheap. Organizing last-minute canvasses and phone banks takes resources — and Small Town PAC is making sure they have what they need to pull them off.
If we don’t back them now, our slate could fall short and lose. It’s as simple as that.
**[Peter, can you chip in $5 to make sure our slate of Democratic fighters for the working class can reach enough voters to win in two days?](https://act.timwalz.com/go/73?c0=stp-ms-em-20261101-1._OARW_&amount=5&refcode=em20261030-1296&t=1&akid=1296%2E34582%2EVJbOkd)**

Tim Walz

name: Voto Latino
subject: Thank you, Peter.
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Voto Latino
body:
1.6 million voters. 22 districts. 6 states. 2 days.
#
Peter,
**We’re just two days away from Election Day, and we want to take a moment to thank you.**
All cycle long, we’ve been sending you updates on our work, and at the same time, your support has been out in the field doing that work: reaching Latino voters in the states and districts that will decide this election. Every text sent, every call made, and every voter who learned where, when, and how to cast their ballot was made possible by people like you.
Here’s where that work is happening right now. We’re on the ground in Arizona, Nevada, North Carolina, Georgia, Pennsylvania, and Texas, and across 22 target congressional districts from coast to coast. In many of these districts, Latino voters make up the margin between winning and losing, and the races could be decided by just a few thousand votes.
That’s why these final two days are so important.
The voters we still need to reach are often the ones who’ve been overlooked the longest: new voters, young voters, and people who’ve been told their voice doesn’t count. A personal text or a phone call from a trusted messenger can be the difference between staying home and showing up. **That’s why we’re going all in, but we’re going to need a final surge of support to help get these races across the finish line.**
**[We can’t do it without you, Peter. Will you chip in $3 or any amount to help us reach Latino voters in this final stretch?](https://act.votolatino.org/go/57?c0=em-ms-voto-20261101-1.TNzvAr&amount=3&refcode=em20261101-741&t=1&akid=741%2E1366028%2EeEGMUV)**

| | November 1, 2026
Lamont, Blanchard and Hughes Incidents Show Their Disdain for the Law
* Don't get in the way of their 'will to power'

In the space of just 12 hours, as this last weekend of campaigning commenced, it was revealed that each of these Democrat candidates' arrogant actions got themselves tangled up with the law.
On Friday, a report made its way into the press that the prior week, Rob Blanchard, candidate for District 28 senate seat for Fairfield, Newtown, Bethel and Easton, was cited for disobeying a patrol officer's instructions for avoiding a road construction site and crashed his car. Blanchard is also Ned Lamont's communications director, as he runs for elective office. Details finally appeared in the Newtown Bee - see [Blanchard](https://lk9rohfbb.cc.rs6.net/tn.jsp?f=001LOZngNu9RwkwEFmlHWv5qph_1153tXjT6dp7UaIVB80Td5YJHTyt_xJ5ZCZXN91uYrT1FtcFrDZYz21ig60w5xELmJxmE4CdOdhIBR6NQ6npi8i1qSlugX1pCdJtURrFtsryRYUN9ppPeXWeUjTdYJYODpziJ0LpXApAyKswN9MnRF_6yTsX7yqwxaqj5E6EAldmYJcKc2V3WMVikXwOE2eC5DUxXBUkzMv70x3znOeEnuaV13EV3ww2fZxCmMkTNpbYE8Fq-mhqttkLfhCKAMUUifmFRkR5DdFyd1bLwFWgy_3zX5sfQi3q8MeyCLfzNZfaMNms9eg=&c=3PCmBSOPF8aR-yNeBMg7pXWZ2pENxCZiyFWmUN2EKxpTJv9m13pMuA==&ch=SaYDp5FnPNPkJaMG6avjolj_rWBrkXPuGz0oSlWELxulK5FEsd72lA==).
As the man in a hurry disregarded police instruction, his front wheel collapsed into a hole and disabled his car. Funny how it took a week for this to make its way to print.
Then Blanchard's comrade, Easton incumbent Democrat State Rep Anne Hughes was arrested Friday night for stealing the campaign signs of her opponent, Republican Darrell Harris, and stashing them in her garage. Turns out team Harris was tired of getting their signs stolen, so they 'air-tagged' a few and Hughes scarfed them up in the dead of night, and the police came tracking and calling. See [Hughes Article](https://lk9rohfbb.cc.rs6.net/tn.jsp?f=001LOZngNu9RwkwEFmlHWv5qph_1153tXjT6dp7UaIVB80Td5YJHTyt_xJ5ZCZXN91ueViG-haxk8usB7F_BqpqVM-tyJtb6heUdYwW-DQ3S8hNMBOntomgt9cBtJUThOjJj2AZ0yde1TmBN3gdDMqZLhT2W3XIjVtXUjeLVHrBEN3321KdzkApuMRov2bLSTDZTJptQyvEXeurTee7ON8IL0lBabIWq0QV4_yfe2-y5eWBZl75CodggGnkVy2EuetP81zvzVA8PIlMPPDFS6eebU9e-FQZEBl_&c=3PCmBSOPF8aR-yNeBMg7pXWZ2pENxCZiyFWmUN2EKxpTJv9m13pMuA==&ch=SaYDp5FnPNPkJaMG6avjolj_rWBrkXPuGz0oSlWELxulK5FEsd72lA==)
Evidently, Hughes feels she MUST get reelected to continue controlling the lives of the citizens of District 135, and can't let a freedom-loving Republican get in her way.
And birds of a feather, Blanchard and Hughes, are such best-buds that they launched their campaigns together. Here's the poster announcing their campaign canvassing kickoff.
---
|
---
Not to be outdone, our nervous governor let his disdain toward independent press show on Saturday when he smacked away a reporter's camera when she asked for a comment on his communication director's (Blanchard) run-in with the Newtown police. (I've seen capitol police detain someone for tapping a Rep's shoulder on the floor of the LOB in Hartford) Directly below is the video Jackie Homan of The Connecticut Centinal was shooting when Lamont got 'spooked' by an uncomfortable inquiry as he arrived for an otherwise controlled event in Stamford.

subject: These 10 judges are building an oligarchy.
disclaimer_text: paid for by the right-wing group behind overturning Roe v
body:
[ https://act.demandjustice.org/go/54940?refcode=em20261101-61951&t=1001&akid=61951%2E1407376%2EWIiTYf ]Demand Justice PAC[ https://act.demandjustice.org/go/54940?refcode=em20261101-61951&t=1002&akid=61951%2E1407376%2EWIiTYf ]Demand Justice PAC

Ten federal
judges. One result: more power for corporations and the ultra-wealthy,
less for everyone else.

Together, they’re enabling the slide toward Oligarchy. Take a look:

#1: Judge Andrew Oldham: called our entire system of administrative law
“constitutionally suspect,” a view that threatens the EPA, OSHA, and the
CFPB.

#2: Chief Judge Reed O’Connor: ruled the entire Affordable Care Act
unconstitutional, a theory so extreme the Supreme Court reversed it 7-2.

#3: Chief Judge Amos Mazzant: struck down overtime pay for 4 million
workers and blocked a law targeting anonymous shell companies.

#4: Judge James C. Ho: reported 26 reimbursed trips, including a Cancun
junket paid for by the right-wing group behind overturning Roe v. Wade.

#5: Judge Don R. Willett: wants to revive the legal doctrine courts once
used to strike down minimum wage and child labor laws.

#6: Judge Edith H. Jones: argued for a theory that would have destroyed
the CFPB, the agency that has returned over $21 billion to consumers.

#7: Judge Victor Marrero: approved the T-Mobile/Sprint merger despite
objections from 14 state attorneys general. The combined company shed
roughly 14,000 jobs.

#8: Judge J. Campbell Barker: helped kill a rule that would have raised
franchise and contract workers’ pay by $1.06 billion a year.

#9: Judge Ada E. Brown: nullified the FTC’s non-compete ban, costing 30
million workers more than $400 billion in wages.

#10: Judge Sean D. Jordan: wiped out overtime protections for another 4
million workers, then killed a rule keeping medical debt off credit
reports.

Workers, consumers, and patients lose. Corporations and billionaires get
richer. Several of these judges have their lifestyles bankrolled by the
same conservative legal network shaping the bench, and we’re calling it
what it is: corruption.

Demand Justice PAC is fighting back: naming names, exposing the money and
influence behind these rulings, and fighting to restore independence to
our courts.

[ https://act.demandjustice.org/go/55459?c0=dj-em-20261101.LiDVc0&refcode=em20261101-61951&amounts=5%2C20%2C50%2C100%2C250%2C500%2C1000&amount=5&t=1003&akid=61951%2E1407376%2EWIiTYf ]We can’t do it without grassroots supporters like you. Will you chip in
$5 today to help us fight the judges enabling the slide
toward Oligarchy?

name: Aaron Ford
subject: I’m no stranger to competitive races
disclaimer_text: Paid for by the Committee to Elect Aaron Ford
body:
# [](https://act.fordfornevada.com/go/12?t=1&akid=1244%2E127862%2EH2TvMM)
Friends,
It’s Sunday, two days out, and I’ve been on the go since I woke up. But in the quiet moments between campaign stops, I keep coming back to one thing — how close this race is going to be.
I’m no stranger to competitive races.
In 2018, I ran for Attorney General. When the votes were counted, I’d won by _fewer than 5,000 votes_ out of nearly a million cast. Less than half a percent.
Think about that. **If a few thousand folks across Nevada had stayed home or figured somebody else would handle it, I wouldn’t have spent the last eight years taking on big drug companies, corporate landlords, and Donald Trump in court.**
I’ve lost, too. In my first race for state Senate, I got beat by about 20 points. I came back two years later and won.
So when I tell you every vote and every dollar matters, know that I mean it 100%.
**[Fuel our final GOTV push by donating today ››](https://act.fordfornevada.com/go/1?c0=em_ms_af_20261101_1_ak.Hb2xr4&amount=5&refcode=em20261101-1227&t=3&akid=1244%2E127862%2EH2TvMM)**
We’ve been at this for months now. Y’all have chipped in, knocked doors, and talked to your neighbors.
In the beginning, we were trailing MAGA Gov. Joe Lombardo by several points. Now, basically every public poll this fall has had us within two points.
**This is our race to win.**
It all comes down to what we do in these final days. Our main focus from now until November 3 is to reach undecided, last-minute voters — **and your $5 fuels that work.**
This is one of the last times I’ll ask before Election Day. **[Will you chip in $5 to help us finish strong?](https://act.fordfornevada.com/go/1?c0=em_ms_af_20261101_1_ak.Hb2xr4&amount=5&refcode=em20261101-1227&t=4&akid=1244%2E127862%2EH2TvMM)**
**[Donate $5 ››](https://act.fordfornevada.com/go/1?c0=em_ms_af_20261101_1_ak.Hb2xr4&amount=5&refcode=em20261101-1227&t=23&akid=1244%2E127862%2EH2TvMM)**
I’ve won close ones before. I know what it takes. Let’s do it again this Tuesday.
With gratitude,
Aaron
[](https://act.fordfornevada.com/go/1?c0=em_ms_af_20261101_1_ak.Hb2xr4&amount=5&refcode=em20261101-1227&t=24&akid=1244%2E127862%2EH2TvMM)
Make a plan to vote on or before November 3! [**Click here for resources ››**](https://act.fordfornevada.com/go/225?t=25&akid=1244%2E127862%2EH2TvMM)

**[Donate](https://secure.actblue.com/donate/em_ms_af_footer?refcode=em20261101-1244-&t=26&refcode2=1244_127862_H2TvMM&akid=1244%2E127862%2EH2TvMM)**

name: John Grisham
subject: James Talarico will challenge our country’s broken status quo.
body:
[ https://act.jamestalarico.com/go/512?c0=jt-em-2026q4.erR9_P&refcode=em261101-3-ak&t=1001&akid=1180%2E1347274%2E9albb5 ]John Grisham

Peter —

I don’t go to bat for many candidates, but I am reaching out today because
I believe we have a historic opportunity to elect a champion for the
people in Texas: James Talarico.

I spend a lot of time thinking and writing about justice in this country —
and how often it is out of reach for working people.

I was born and raised in the Deep South. We didn’t have much. My parents
didn’t have a formal education, but they worked hard to make sure we had
enough and gave us every opportunity they could to get ahead.

Today, stories like mine are a lot harder to come by. Too many families
struggle to even make ends meet, and for a lot of folks, the opportunities
I got are out of reach entirely.

The status quo is rigged in favor of billionaires and powerful corporate
interests, and it’s no accident.

We have corporate interests, billionaires, and now even a trillionaire
spending limitless sums to keep this broken system intact. They pour money
into super PACs to buy politicians.

And like any Texan right now could tell you, all that money goes toward
endless, outrageous attack ads. The lies about James are an astounding
distortion of the truth.

It’s a system designed to work for those at the top and keep the rest of
us fighting each other. But like James says, our fight is not left vs.
right — it’s top vs. bottom.

If enough of us come together and demand change, we can win and change our
country forever. That starts this year with James’ race in Texas. Nothing
would shake up the status quo and give people hope more than seeing this
people-powered movement flip Texas.

We cannot expect our broken system to fix itself. We have to fight for it.
So I’m asking you to be part of that:

[ https://act.jamestalarico.com/go/512?c0=jt-em-2026q4.erR9_P&refcode=em261101-3-ak&t=1002&akid=1180%2E1347274%2E9albb5 ]Will you please donate anything you can to James Talarico’s campaign
today? Elon Musk and his billionaire cronies are spending over $300
million to buy this seat, and it’s up to us to stop them.

[ https://act.jamestalarico.com/go/512?c0=jt-em-2026q4.erR9_P&refcode=em261101-3-ak&t=1003&akid=1180%2E1347274%2E9albb5 ]CONTRIBUTE

Thank you,

John Grisham

[ https://act.jamestalarico.com/go/512?c0=jt-em-2026q4.erR9_P&refcode=em261101-3-ak&t=1004&akid=1180%2E1347274%2E9albb5 ]'New York Times: In Texas, Talarico Inspires a Recurring Blue-Tinted
Dream In the go-big-or-go-home collective consciousness of Texas, no
ambition is deemed too reckless, no daydream too wild. Save perhaps one.
It is the idea, fantastical to many as it is irresistible to others, that
the Democrats will win a statewide race in Texas for the first time in 32
years. According to the latest New York Times/Siena University poll of the
race for U.S. Senate, James Talarico, a 37-year-old state legislator seen
by national Democrats as one of the breakout stars of this cycle, is ahead
of his Republican rival, Ken Paxton, the state’s scandal-plagued attorney
general, by six points. The poll was conducted from Sept. 21 to Sept. 30.
A survey from mid-September, the ReconMR/Siena Research Institute poll,
also showed the Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Gina Hinojosa, four
points ahead of the three-term G.O.P. incumbent, Greg Abbott, the most
dominant political figure in Texas. Cue the fluttering heartbeats. Cue, as
well, the eye-rolls. Given how thoroughly Republicans have dominated the
state, and how the hopes of Democrats have repeatedly crashed, some Texas
pollsters remain skeptical. “At some point, you do get conditioned by all
that’s happened in the past,” said James Henson, the director of the
University of Texas at Austin’s Texas Politics Project. “I mean, you look
at the trends and you have to admit that something’s going on. But you
still don’t want to believe your lying eyes, because you’ve been burned
for so long.” Mr. Henson was referring to the perennial spectacle of
much-ballyhooed Texas Democratic aspirants face-planting against the Lone
Star State’s red wall. First came Tony Sanchez Jr., the swaggering and
self-funding Laredo oilman whom Gov. Rick Perry dispatched in 2002 by an
18-point margin. Next was the state senator Wendy Davis, who attracted
worldwide attention for her filibuster in the Texas Legislature against an
anti-abortion measure but whom Mr. Abbott demolished by 20 points in 2014.
Finally, the El Paso congressman Beto O’Rourke came up 2.6 points short of
defeating Senator Ted Cruz in 2018 but then suffered a 10-point loss to
Mr. Abbott four years later. Even with the awareness of such humiliations,
Democrats find themselves maintaining that 2026 could, at long last, be
the year. President Trump’s deep unpopularity and the prospect of a blue
wave could, they insist, extend into the state he won by nearly 14 points
in 2024. According to a September survey conducted by Texas Southern
University, Mr. Trump is seven points underwater in Texas. Mr. Talarico
has run an energetic and well-financed campaign, while Mr. Paxton has
staged far fewer public events and has had to rely on outside groups to
fund an attack-ad blitzkrieg against his Democratic opponent. Mr. Abbott,
meanwhile, has outspent Ms. Hinojosa by a 10-to-one ratio, yet has been
unable to build an insurmountable lead. “People have vastly underestimated
Gina,” said Ms. Davis, now a political consultant and a senior adviser to
Planned Parenthood Texas Votes, an advocacy organization. “Dollar for
dollar, she’s running the best statewide campaign we’ve ever seen.” Such
optimism stands in defiance of the political axiom that Texas is where
idealistic Democrats go to be mugged by reality. The party’s demise there
is not a product of ill fortune, Mr. Henson said. “Governor Abbott has
built an impressive election machine that has benefited state-level
Republicans again and again for a decade and a half,” he said. “And the
Democratic machinery here is almost nonexistent.” A ‘Hollowing-Out’ I have
written about the politics of my native state at regular intervals for
more than three decades. After watching the Democrats’ century-long rule
in Texas come to a decisive end with Gov. Ann Richards’s loss to George W.
Bush in 1994, I saw the party descend into atrophy in which failure begot
more failure. “The 30-year drought has done a lot of things,” said Luke
Warford, the chairman of the Travis County Democratic Party and the
founder of the Agave Democratic Infrastructure Fund. “It’s kept donors on
the sidelines, which makes a lot of potentially good candidates not run
because there’s no belief they can win. And it also makes a lot of really
talented staff leave to find better-paying work in true battleground
states.” The Democratic Party has no counterpart to Mr. Abbott, and hasn’t
since 1993, when Senator Lloyd Bentsen moved to Washington to join
President Bill Clinton’s cabinet. Its weaknesses are even more glaring
farther down the hierarchy. In recent elections, as many as one-third of
state races have gone uncontested by Democrats. One-fifth of the party’s
county chairs and two-thirds of its precinct chairs have been left
unfilled. Until last year, the state party had a negative operating
budget. As the veteran Democratic consultant Matt Angle observed, “There’s
been a hollowing-out of the party.” Still, those of us who recall the
satisfied sense of invincibility among Texas Democrats after roughly a
century of one-party rule have detected similar signs of overconfidence
among the state’s ruling party. The party’s rightward tilt, increasingly
forceful with each legislative session, reached its apotheosis in March,
with Mr. Paxton’s primary victory over the more moderate Republican
four-term incumbent, Senator John Cornyn. Mr. Paxton, a close ally of Mr.
Trump’s, was impeached by the Republican-controlled State House (and later
acquitted by the State Senate) in 2023 over allegations that included
bribery. He was also accused by his wife of adultery. Mr. Trump endorsed
him anyway, all but guaranteeing his landslide primary triumph over Mr.
Cornyn but in the process testing the allegiance of center-right Texans.
In similar fashion, the Texas G.O.P. is in danger of losing many Latino
voters who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 after years of siding with
Democrats. “We adopted a lazy way of campaigning that bit us on the ass,
and we’ve learned from that,” Mr. O’Rourke said. “Now it’s the Republicans
who’ve gotten really lazy and complacent and comfortable.” Signs of
Republican Overreach Simply spending one week driving through the vastness
of Texas, as I did in September, is all it takes to appreciate an underdog
party’s uphill battle. The state’s 32 million residents are spread across
20 media markets, many of them distinct ecosystems, from the urban colossi
of Houston and the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex to the oil patch of the
Texas Panhandle to the Latino-dominated borderlands of the Rio Grande
Valley. “When national donors are deciding where to invest, they look at a
place like Iowa, where $5 million can fully fund a race,” said Katherine
Fischer, the director of the Texas Majority PAC, which was established by
the liberal philanthropist Soros family. “That’s why Texas is always at
the bottom of their list. It’s just so damned big.” Reaching so many
markets presents a daunting challenge for an upstart candidate like Ms.
Hinojosa, a state representative from the border city of Brownsville.
“There’s still 20 percent of the electorate that doesn’t know who I am,”
she said in an interview in mid-September. To date, Ms. Hinojosa’s
campaign has said that it has raised about $20 million. For his part, Mr.
Talarico spent about $30 million earlier this year to introduce himself
statewide as a man of Christian faith and a member of the Texas House with
a record of supporting bipartisan legislation. Since that time, however,
Mr. Paxton and his associates have invested more than $100 million in an
effort to redefine his opponent as “radical” and “weird,” with ads that
quote from remarks Mr. Talarico made several years ago (and later
renounced) suggesting that “God is nonbinary” and that there are six
biological sexes. Mr. Paxton and his allies have at times questioned Mr.
Talarico’s manhood and even his Christianity, an effort to jolt the
sensibilities of a state prone to mythologizing godly and masculine
archetypes. “How they’re negatively defining Talarico is kind of a
bank-shot way of saying that he’s not a true Texas conservative,” Mr.
Henson said. Whether money can overwhelm conditions on the ground is the
riddle looming over the Texas races. In the border city of Laredo, which
Mr. Trump won in 2024 — the first time a Republican had done so in over a
century — signs of buyer’s remorse are evident. Arrests by Immigration and
Customs Enforcement agents in Laredo were higher in July than in any other
American city. Mr. Trump’s erratic trade policies have further created
instability at the city’s port of entry. While acknowledging the economic
concerns that many border residents share, Adrian Zapata, a business
executive in the health industry who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, said in
an interview that the negative ads against Mr. Talarico were resonating
with some of his family members. “They see Talarico as an ultraliberal,”
he said. “They’re done with the ‘they/them.’ They’re going to vote for
Paxton just because of that.” As for Mr. Zapata, “I’m not ready to vote
for Talarico,” he said. “But I don’t like Paxton. He’s never done anything
for South Texas, and his personal and business dealings have hurt him a
lot with folks down here.” There is a similarly muddled electoral picture
in the cattle country of deep West Texas adjacent to Big Bend National
Park. Mr. Trump and Mr. Abbott have aggressively championed a border wall
and artificial intelligence data centers, both of which threaten to
disrupt the region’s pastoral ethos. A coalition of more than 200
landowners has sued the federal government over the border wall, while
other residents have circulated a petition to protest the construction of
a new data center near Fort Stockton. George Johnson, a cattle feed
operator in Alpine, waved off such concerns, saying: “Folks worrying about
data centers were also worried when the internet got started. It’s
Talarico who scares me to death, him and all that socialist talk.” Others
in this largely conservative region harbor the view that Republicans have
failed to make good on their promises. Thaddeus Cleveland, the Republican
sheriff of Terrell County, said that both he and his county had voted for
Mr. Trump in 2024, but added, “Everything he campaigned on, we’re seeing
the opposite of, like going to war.” Sheriff Cleveland predicted that the
negative campaign ads by the Republicans would not factor as significantly
into the votes of his neighbors as “the price of groceries and gas, which
are compounded here because we’re so far from everywhere else.” But it is
in purple Tarrant County, dominated by Fort Worth, where the party could
pay the price for having potentially overestimated its mandate from the
voters. Conservative leaders have cut funds for nonprofits that aid
at-risk children, subjected school library books to right-wing litmus
tests and eliminated free bus rides to polling stations in poor
neighborhoods. “The far-right leaders here have implemented Project 2025
on a county level,” said Alisa Simmons, a Democrat and county commissioner
who is running to unseat the conservative county judge, Tim O’Hare. In an
early sign this year that area Republicans may be out of step with Tarrant
County’s constituents, a Democratic aviation machinist and union leader,
Taylor Rehmet, defeated Leigh Wambsganss, a well-funded Republican
Christian activist who led the conservative takeover of several metroplex
school boards. He won by 14 points in a January special election for a
State Senate seat covering a region that Mr. Trump won by 17 points in
2024. A ‘Gradualist’ Theory Which party prevails in Texas is a complicated
riddle. Historically a low-turnout state — it ranked second to last in the
2024 election, ahead of only Arkansas — Texas held a primary in March that
saw nearly one in four voters showing up to the polls, a modern record for
midterm participation, with Democrats slightly outpacing Republicans. A
few factors could conspire to thwart a blue wave in Texas. As of 2020,
straight-ticket voting is no longer possible in the state, which could
impact the mostly Democratic urban counties where that practice has
frequently been used by voters in past elections. Texas is one of only
eight states that lack universal online registration, while voting by mail
is also highly restricted. In January, Mr. Abbott turned over the state’s
list of approximately 18.7 million registered voters to the Trump
administration, and 1.2 million of them have subsequently been put on the
“suspense list” because their addresses have not been verified. The recent
shuttering of nearly one-third of Tarrant County’s polling sites by its
Republican-controlled county commission is particularly worrisome for
Democrats. “The reason we’ve lost these statewide races in the past is
because we’ve never gotten enough out of Tarrant County to overcome the
margins in rural Texas,” Ms. Davis said of the turnout. “If we don’t get
it to 53 or 54 percent this November, it’s game over. James and Gina can’t
win.” But the state’s Republicans have reasons of their own to be fretful.
Partly because of the recruitment efforts of the Texas Majority PAC and
Blueprint Texas, a down-ballot candidate support organization co-founded
by Ms. Davis earlier this year, the Democrats are fielding a full slate in
all 150 state races for the first time in a half-century. Though many of
these aspirants face long odds, their presence on the ballot could
energize the Democrats in predominantly conservative regions who have not
bothered to turn out in the past. “If we win on Nov. 3, most of those
names running down-ballot in really tough areas like East Texas and the
Hill Country and the Panhandle will be responsible,” Mr. O’Rourke said.
Mr. Henson added that while he remained skeptical about Democratic
enthusiasm being sufficient to carry the day for Mr. Talarico, he also
doubted that a last-minute avalanche of negative ads would prove decisive
for Mr. Paxton. “At a certain point, there’s diminishing impact once you
get past an absurd level of spending,” he said. Rather than project a
winner in November, Mr. Henson said he felt more comfortable embracing a
“gradualist” theory, one in which Texas does not become blue overnight,
but instead competitive. “Even if Talarico loses by a Beto-like margin,”
he said, “the next cycle is a presidential election, where Trump likely
won’t be popular and Democratic turnout will be higher. So there are

[ ]CONTRIBUTE Thank you, John Grisham [ ]'New York Times: In Texas, Talarico Inspires a Recurring Blue-Tinted Dream In the go-big-or-go-home collective consciousness of Texas, no ambition is deemed too reckless, no daydream too wild. Save perhaps one. It is the idea, fantastical to many as it is irresistible to others, that the Democrats will win a statewide race in Texas for the first time in 32 years. According to the latest New York Times/Siena University poll of the race for U.S. Senate, James Talarico, a 37-year-old state legislator seen by national Democrats as one of the breakout stars of this cycle, is ahead of his Republican rival, Ken Paxton, the state’s scandal-plagued attorney general, by six points. The poll was conducted from Sept. 21 to Sept. 30. A survey from mid-September, the ReconMR/Siena Research Institute poll, also showed the Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Gina Hinojosa, four points ahead of the three-term G.O.P. incumbent, Greg Abbott, the most dominant political figure in Texas. Cue the fluttering heartbeats. Cue, as well, the eye-rolls. Given how thoroughly Republicans have dominated the state, and how the hopes of Democrats have repeatedly crashed, some Texas pollsters remain skeptical. “At some point, you do get conditioned by all that’s happened in the past,” said James Henson, the director of the University of Texas at Austin’s Texas Politics Project. “I mean, you look at the trends and you have to admit that something’s going on. But you still don’t want to believe your lying eyes, because you’ve been burned for so long.” Mr. Henson was referring to the perennial spectacle of much-ballyhooed Texas Democratic aspirants face-planting against the Lone Star State’s red wall. First came Tony Sanchez Jr., the swaggering and self-funding Laredo oilman whom Gov. Rick Perry dispatched in 2002 by an 18-point margin. Next was the state senator Wendy Davis, who attracted worldwide attention for her filibuster in the Texas Legislature against an anti-abortion measure but whom Mr. Abbott demolished by 20 points in 2014. Finally, the El Paso congressman Beto O’Rourke came up 2.6 points short of defeating Senator Ted Cruz in 2018 but then suffered a 10-point loss to Mr. Abbott four years later. Even with the awareness of such humiliations, Democrats find themselves maintaining that 2026 could, at long last, be the year. President Trump’s deep unpopularity and the prospect of a blue wave could, they insist, extend into the state he won by nearly 14 points in 2024. According to a September survey conducted by Texas Southern University, Mr. Trump is seven points underwater in Texas. Mr. Talarico has run an energetic and well-financed campaign, while Mr. Paxton has staged far fewer public events and has had to rely on outside groups to fund an attack-ad blitzkrieg against his Democratic opponent. Mr. Abbott, meanwhile, has outspent Ms. Hinojosa by a 10-to-one ratio, yet has been unable to build an insurmountable lead. “People have vastly underestimated Gina,” said Ms. Davis, now a political consultant and a senior adviser to Planned Parenthood Texas Votes, an advocacy organization. “Dollar for dollar, she’s running the best statewide campaign we’ve ever seen.” Such optimism stands in defiance of the political axiom that Texas is where idealistic Democrats go to be mugged by reality. The party’s demise there is not a product of ill fortune, Mr. Henson said. “Governor Abbott has built an impressive election machine that has benefited state-level Republicans again and again for a decade and a half,” he said. “And the Democratic machinery here is almost nonexistent.” A ‘Hollowing-Out’ I have written about the politics of my native state at regular intervals for more than three decades. After watching the Democrats’ century-long rule in Texas come to a decisive end with Gov. Ann Richards’s loss to George W. Bush in 1994, I saw the party descend into atrophy in which failure begot more failure. “The 30-year drought has done a lot of things,” said Luke Warford, the chairman of the Travis County Democratic Party and the founder of the Agave Democratic Infrastructure Fund. “It’s kept donors on the sidelines, which makes a lot of potentially good candidates not run because there’s no belief they can win. And it also makes a lot of really talented staff leave to find better-paying work in true battleground states.” The Democratic Party has no counterpart to Mr. Abbott, and hasn’t since 1993, when Senator Lloyd Bentsen moved to Washington to join President Bill Clinton’s cabinet. Its weaknesses are even more glaring farther down the hierarchy. In recent elections, as many as one-third of state races have gone uncontested by Democrats. One-fifth of the party’s county chairs and two-thirds of its precinct chairs have been left unfilled. Until last year, the state party had a negative operating budget. As the veteran Democratic consultant Matt Angle observed, “There’s been a hollowing-out of the party.” Still, those of us who recall the satisfied sense of invincibility among Texas Democrats after roughly a century of one-party rule have detected similar signs of overconfidence among the state’s ruling party. The party’s rightward tilt, increasingly forceful with each legislative session, reached its apotheosis in March, with Mr. Paxton’s primary victory over the more moderate Republican four-term incumbent, Senator John Cornyn. Mr. Paxton, a close ally of Mr. Trump’s, was impeached by the Republican-controlled State House (and later acquitted by the State Senate) in 2023 over allegations that included bribery. He was also accused by his wife of adultery. Mr. Trump endorsed him anyway, all but guaranteeing his landslide primary triumph over Mr. Cornyn but in the process testing the allegiance of center-right Texans. In similar fashion, the Texas G.O.P. is in danger of losing many Latino voters who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 after years of siding with Democrats. “We adopted a lazy way of campaigning that bit us on the ass, and we’ve learned from that,” Mr. O’Rourke said. “Now it’s the Republicans who’ve gotten really lazy and complacent and comfortable.” Signs of Republican Overreach Simply spending one week driving through the vastness of Texas, as I did in September, is all it takes to appreciate an underdog party’s uphill battle. The state’s 32 million residents are spread across 20 media markets, many of them distinct ecosystems, from the urban colossi of Houston and the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex to the oil patch of the Texas Panhandle to the Latino-dominated borderlands of the Rio Grande Valley. “When national donors are deciding where to invest, they look at a place like Iowa, where $5 million can fully fund a race,” said Katherine Fischer, the director of the Texas Majority PAC, which was established by the liberal philanthropist Soros family. “That’s why Texas is always at the bottom of their list. It’s just so damned big.” Reaching so many markets presents a daunting challenge for an upstart candidate like Ms. Hinojosa, a state representative from the border city of Brownsville. “There’s still 20 percent of the electorate that doesn’t know who I am,” she said in an interview in mid-September. To date, Ms. Hinojosa’s campaign has said that it has raised about $20 million. For his part, Mr. Talarico spent about $30 million earlier this year to introduce himself statewide as a man of Christian faith and a member of the Texas House with a record of supporting bipartisan legislation. Since that time, however, Mr. Paxton and his associates have invested more than $100 million in an effort to redefine his opponent as “radical” and “weird,” with ads that quote from remarks Mr. Talarico made several years ago (and later renounced) suggesting that “God is nonbinary” and that there are six biological sexes. Mr. Paxton and his allies have at times questioned Mr. Talarico’s manhood and even his Christianity, an effort to jolt the sensibilities of a state prone to mythologizing godly and masculine archetypes. “How they’re negatively defining Talarico is kind of a bank-shot way of saying that he’s not a true Texas conservative,” Mr. Henson said. Whether money can overwhelm conditions on the ground is the riddle looming over the Texas races. In the border city of Laredo, which Mr. Trump won in 2024 — the first time a Republican had done so in over a century — signs of buyer’s remorse are evident. Arrests by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in Laredo were higher in July than in any other American city. Mr. Trump’s erratic trade policies have further created instability at the city’s port of entry. While acknowledging the economic concerns that many border residents share, Adrian Zapata, a business executive in the health industry who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, said in an interview that the negative ads against Mr. Talarico were resonating with some of his family members. “They see Talarico as an ultraliberal,” he said. “They’re done with the ‘they/them.’ They’re going to vote for Paxton just because of that.” As for Mr. Zapata, “I’m not ready to vote for Talarico,” he said. “But I don’t like Paxton. He’s never done anything for South Texas, and his personal and business dealings have hurt him a lot with folks down here.” There is a similarly muddled electoral picture in the cattle country of deep West Texas adjacent to Big Bend National Park. Mr. Trump and Mr. Abbott have aggressively championed a border wall and artificial intelligence data centers, both of which threaten to disrupt the region’s pastoral ethos. A coalition of more than 200 landowners has sued the federal government over the border wall, while other residents have circulated a petition to protest the construction of a new data center near Fort Stockton. George Johnson, a cattle feed operator in Alpine, waved off such concerns, saying: “Folks worrying about data centers were also worried when the internet got started. It’s Talarico who scares me to death, him and all that socialist talk.” Others in this largely conservative region harbor the view that Republicans have failed to make good on their promises. Thaddeus Cleveland, the Republican sheriff of Terrell County, said that both he and his county had voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, but added, “Everything he campaigned on, we’re seeing the opposite of, like going to war.” Sheriff Cleveland predicted that the negative campaign ads by the Republicans would not factor as significantly into the votes of his neighbors as “the price of groceries and gas, which are compounded here because we’re so far from everywhere else.” But it is in purple Tarrant County, dominated by Fort Worth, where the party could pay the price for having potentially overestimated its mandate from the voters. Conservative leaders have cut funds for nonprofits that aid at-risk children, subjected school library books to right-wing litmus tests and eliminated free bus rides to polling stations in poor neighborhoods. “The far-right leaders here have implemented Project 2025 on a county level,” said Alisa Simmons, a Democrat and county commissioner who is running to unseat the conservative county judge, Tim O’Hare. In an early sign this year that area Republicans may be out of step with Tarrant County’s constituents, a Democratic aviation machinist and union leader, Taylor Rehmet, defeated Leigh Wambsganss, a well-funded Republican Christian activist who led the conservative takeover of several metroplex school boards. He won by 14 points in a January special election for a State Senate seat covering a region that Mr. Trump won by 17 points in 2024. A ‘Gradualist’ Theory Which party prevails in Texas is a complicated riddle. Historically a low-turnout state — it ranked second to last in the 2024 election, ahead of only Arkansas — Texas held a primary in March that saw nearly one in four voters showing up to the polls, a modern record for midterm participation, with Democrats slightly outpacing Republicans. A few factors could conspire to thwart a blue wave in Texas. As of 2020, straight-ticket voting is no longer possible in the state, which could impact the mostly Democratic urban counties where that practice has frequently been used by voters in past elections. Texas is one of only eight states that lack universal online registration, while voting by mail is also highly restricted. In January, Mr. Abbott turned over the state’s list of approximately 18.7 million registered voters to the Trump administration, and 1.2 million of them have subsequently been put on the “suspense list” because their addresses have not been verified. The recent shuttering of nearly one-third of Tarrant County’s polling sites by its Republican-controlled county commission is particularly worrisome for Democrats. “The reason we’ve lost these statewide races in the past is because we’ve never gotten enough out of Tarrant County to overcome the margins in rural Texas,” Ms. Davis said of the turnout. “If we don’t get it to 53 or 54 percent this November, it’s game over. James and Gina can’t win.” But the state’s Republicans have reasons of their own to be fretful. Partly because of the recruitment efforts of the Texas Majority PAC and Blueprint Texas, a down-ballot candidate support organization co-founded by Ms. Davis earlier this year, the Democrats are fielding a full slate in all 150 state races for the first time in a half-century. Though many of these aspirants face long odds, their presence on the ballot could energize the Democrats in predominantly conservative regions who have not bothered to turn out in the past. “If we win on Nov. 3, most of those names running down-ballot in really tough areas like East Texas and the Hill Country and the Panhandle will be responsible,” Mr. O’Rourke said. Mr. Henson added that while he remained skeptical about Democratic enthusiasm being sufficient to carry the day for Mr. Talarico, he also doubted that a last-minute avalanche of negative ads would prove decisive for Mr. Paxton. “At a certain point, there’s diminishing impact once you get past an absurd level of spending,” he said. name: Jen Kiggans

body:
People often ask...how did I get that name?

People often ask...how did I get that name?
| [](https://trk.email.repdailyred.__NW2w)
---
That's a picture of me from when I flew H-46 and H-3 helicopters in the U.S. Navy. If you look to my left, you can see my call sign...**Blossom.**
People often ask...how did I get that name?
Well, my roommate in flight school and I went on a bit of a "girl power" kick one day and bought old bathtub non-skid flower stickers from the store, cut out that flower shape in reflective tape from our squadron, and stuck those reflective flowers on our helmets.
There is very little room for making a Navy flight suit more "feminine," but on cruise we were able to be a little more creative and came to love those girly flowers on our helmets.
Although the helicopter community doesn't use call signs as much as some of the fixed wing squadrons, the "Blossom" stuck and was painted on the side of a CH-46 for part of my first cruise. Made for a great photo and story!
It was my experience in the Navy that helped instill in me the importance of service.
Far too often, our elected officials today forget that their job is to SERVE. They think it is their job to tell everyone what to do and why everyone else is wrong....but that's not service.
As a Navy veteran and nurse practitioner, I got so frustrated and decided to run for Congress because I wanted to actually SERVE my country and my community.
**While for some it is all about power, for me it is all about service.**
Sadly, this has made me some enemies in Washington.
No one is going to buy me off or tell me what to do...I'm going to keep serving the people I represent, not serve some "master" in Washington, D.C.
If you are also tired of leaders who care more about power than service, [I'm asking you to send me some help today.](https://trk.email.repdailyred._)
Because I'm a veteran and not a career politician, I need all the help I can get to support my fight against the Democrats.
---
| [RUSH SUPPORT TO JEN](https://trk.email.repdailyred._-f8XwE6sXCUL9thkw)
---
I know this was a longer message than you are probably used to getting, but I want you to know where I'm coming from and why I need your help. Whether it's $100 or just $10, anything you can contribute will help this Navy veteran keep fighting back business as usual in D.C.
It's time we support leaders who truly want to serve our country, and that's what I promise to always do...are you with me, Peter?
With the courage to fight,
---
[](https://trk.email.repdailyred._-_ZyMv65e6Z2EMHqJQ9gQ)
---
-Jen
---

---
[](https://trk.email.repdailyred.)
---
I would not be where I am today without the help of my incredible and faithful supporters like you. Because of your support, I can keep fighting to make our country stronger.

Together we will get our country back on the right track and secure America's success!
---
| [SUPPORT JEN KIGGANS](https://trk.email.repdailyred.)

## Lee Names Interim Prison Chief
Gov. Bill Lee [tapped Christopher Hansen to lead Tennessee’s prison system](https://email.editor.thetennesseeflyover.com/c/eJykkLGupSAURb9GO24AQaSgmMbuTTulQTh4Tx7CC5xo5u8n3l-YcmcnK3uvP1_bl8eM5fjtT3BEaStw9wxE0LbkvwFOj_nyJULbMVOHUEvdJJczE4JxsflAeMGm_BjdLoX1KozghLGTnsQkl_HtQMs0TyAWDdGE2Uaj9qAWy41Ms1BhRPcAheBCCL4o8zIgrJ5nDVNI1vo4KA4RqbYXvYGgFOgdIOW_9YL2CvUcs3sT_fRh-jXIdZDrfd-ve8dPOcjVN8KQYZDr82-QaydPTzzqxXbMmWUAVuBmWAganoxiDSzU88TesRZoLDVfvlmn5qNnDToe5SFpwTwPkesUmJ6SYUpbzizngSUruAVj9yWksbn4c2PO2GczKH48Yj_T6T-9X07-CwAA__-ZhZcx) on an interim basis Friday, weeks after former Commissioner Frank Strada resigned. The shake-up traces back to Sept. 30, when Christa Pike [survived two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital](https://email.editor.thetennesseeflyover.com/c/eJykkLturTAQRb_GdEZ-8DgULm5Dd26bEhl7fBjF2MieQPL3ESnyA2mmma21t9bbc3lajJhe_-0OhigsCa4agQjKEuw7wG4xnjZ5KCtGquByyosSauBSciEX6whPWDrbeLMqOdnONWDkOOleS60ezWbCuPreKmW9EP1DrHJ1o--cG_Q6-qBFg-YGSimklOLRje0IcuqHoQftwjRZzzoBHimXljYgSAlqBQjxK59QWpf3JpqN6KhM_2NqZmq-rqu96n7eT6bmm8_ULAVTs77PK598xRh5BOD2ODImqtxtBSvlY4PCN5sqJI6JoODOf1u5h4O4y6WAI8yJu7zvWCvmBIXbQFB4sBjBc_gE93FnmJqbYvxxYYxYh5F14nWL_ZlOf_R-GvUdAAD__0ucm14) during an attempt to execute her. Lee halted executions while an independent review examines what went wrong. Hansen, who joined the Tennessee Department of Correction in 2023, will run it while [keeping his day job overseeing probation and parole](https://email.editor.thetennesseeflyover.com/c/eJykkD1ywyAQRk-DOjws-i8o0qhz2pQaDCtrJwg0sJbj22fkIhdIvfu-mfe-rvPVUqB4_7QbGuZljvgsAZkxz4v9RtwshcNGj_lGgQu6FNOsle4kgFQwW8d04NzYypubhtE2rkID_Vi3NdR6qFYzePTKQTO0Xa39ALDg0A921Ap8V7uxInMOAigAUEPTX3qEse26Fmu3jKP1olHoiVO-8IqMMWIpiEt4pQPzxaWtCmZl3ouoP4SehJ6W9AP9eRF6OpWEnkJyNgg9_fHyfuIxZXmjEGRAlHbfE0Uu0q2ZCqd9xSxXGwtGSZEx0yZd2jYqhVLELD3uNvOGkaVLOaNjSlGyT-7994jEL1keO-aDTqTKxu9PCoFK14tG3c--bwP-Z_7D6N8AAAD__-NqoJs). That operation has about 1,100 employees statewide. He previously led a county probation department in California and served as the [top federal probation officer in Nevada](https://email.editor.thetennesseeflyover.com/c/eJykkD2u3SAQRleDOywG_FtQpHF306a0MB7fOwoGC0ZY2X3kV7wNvOYrz3d0_rzWl6NA8f3bnWiZjzXiXQIyY14P9xfxdBSqizvmjQIX9CmmVSs9SACpYHWeqeLauWa3m4bZdb5BC-NsegNGT83Hms1No-s8GDRqHo6p32YNiOMxKTDj3pB9gAAKANTUje2IMPfD0KPxxzy7XXQKd-KUW_4gY4xYCuIR_qWKufXpbIL9MF9FmF9CL0Iv9323dw3cchV6efBCL6CEXswz71TlRiHIgCjddSWKXCRFxkyn9Ok8qRRKEbP8vpM7Xi7ziZGlTzmjZ0qxCL002e7XTSFQGUbRqfcT7UuLf9i0Wv0_AAD__1R4jQs). ## Fake Email Claims Hemp Rules Lifted
A fake email posing as a [Tennessee Alcoholic Beverage Commission (TABC)](https://email.editor.thetennesseeflyover.com/c/eJykkb2O3DAQg5_G7mYhyX_rwkUad5c2pTGWxuvJ6ucgTSzk7QOnSJPyWhIk8JE_PrYPZM_x9R0DLSLHFqkWTyKUtwPfRAHZXxgd5Z29FLIpps0oM4LWoPSGVviircfWLbvRM_a2pUVPczd0ujPP9lysngxpsw9TNx6KkOzQIXXjU_eoTK9aXu5CrZXWWj376TGRnodxHKizxzyja3pFjiXlh5wkFCOVQnT43-mi_LAptH45RT5L031rzNqYtdb6qO8cb7Mx603VmPVfFP4T0Nt0Js8Wdroo44vAphC4FE4RPB9SIJMge_AcWAqkCHJaBEdeEGbA6OCdUVIAizHizgUOnyplCJj55y-MCJXINWZt8-I-K3vPZZyaXr3umf-CyBdfuBbzJwAA___ZWKF2) notice told licensed retailers Saturday morning that all restrictions on hemp products had been lifted. The message, [sent on what looked like official TABC letterhead](https://email.editor.thetennesseeflyover.com/c/eJyk0L3uozAQBPCnMR2INTYfhYs0KE2idFeijb0OVoyNYA_u3v7EvcK_H82Mfr8e0wNDDOnzxIUMs58SnXskZtomj1-iBUM8MDna3iHyTjanPMlatiVAWcOElsNBk8LCmbeEAZUtyEA3NLqBRvbFbKzXtrWIRL5DRz36ptO9Hix5JOVsEcxVCFADQN2rruoIBt22mhrrhwGdUDW5wHmreCamlGjfiXz8mw_aKpuXIpqZed1FcxNyFHI8z7OyMzJjyvmD6QoJOV47Qo5QCzk2IOSopVadEnK8Y4z5JErla8P0LZ-5vMVY3mlZy9eW3W_LFe7rn2Izbj1DjGFvO6HqzwX0_wL_0O8w8l8AAAD__04JhKI), said stores could sell THCA, Delta-8, Delta-9, and other hemp products at any strength, claiming to undo the THCA ban that took effect July 1. It also cleared kratom for sale and made routine store inspections optional. Aaron Rummage, the commission’s policy and communications director, said the email came from an unidentified outside party. “ _Hemp restrictions remain in effect,”_ he said. In a follow-up notice to licensees, the commission said the fake email also claimed licensing accounts had been deleted, and it warned recipients not to click any links or reply. TABC’s laws, product limits, and inspection requirements all still stand.
## Vanderbilt's $7 Billion Tennessee Impact
Vanderbilt University generates an estimated [$7 billion a year in economic activity](https://email.editor.thetennesseeflyover.com/c/eJykkLFugzAQhp_GbEY-G0wYPHRhS9eOyJgjOdU2Eb6A8vYVGdoH6HLS6aT__u_7uo5XT5Hy7dMndMzLmPEoEZlxGxf_jZg8xd3nGbeJIhcMa15HrbSVAFLB6APTjmPjq9lNGnrfhAoddL1pDRh9qe4OQfcWrLbe2BlNC97itCzawsX2oVEVuTMQQAGAujRd3SH0rbUtmrD0vZ9Fo3AmXrea78iYM5aCuMTXuuNWhzVV0d2ZH0WYD6EHoYfjOOqjpP08Cj2c-UIPoIQezDkKP-eXxMKUPGORf4jymWnHrRC_ivz9Jd_giYKk9PCBZScnipHWLPRQbW5-HOdabCcadTulvWvxP53uTv8EAAD__xv8jJ0) across Tennessee and supports 43,677 jobs, a new study found. Of that, $4 billion is direct spending. The biggest piece, $2.3 billion, comes from the higher earnings of Vanderbilt alumni living in Tennessee, followed by [$1.2 billion in university operations, $270 million in capital projects, and $146 million students spend](https://email.editor.thetennesseeflyover.com/c/eJykkLGu4yAQRb8Gd1iAsR0Kim3cZdstrTEMCVoMFsw62r9_coqXD3jNVKN7zz1_7usdYor58Rt2tERhzfhqCYmwrgH-Iu4Q0wnZY91iooau5LIqoSYuJRdyBUfxxFVD5-2mpAHtOrRyNsM4yEHduqdVxuA031Rwg_YiGDWC3jbQo5MGYIIu2itQSiGlFDc99zNKM07TiIMLxoBnWqCPVGpPTyTMGVtDDOl_ObH2ruxdsk-io7HhF1MLU8s1o_9w9-j_MbVcNUwtUlzHMLV8PvgDM1YgbHzmW0wplsxj5u_Be3Q87gc44uBqaY1_Q_CML17xKJV4iNk3ppauWn-8row2zUyLxyXxjUk_dHxa9RUAAP__mbqSrQ) off campus on housing, meals, and other purchases. The Tennessee Independent Colleges and Universities Association, which represents 34 private schools including Vanderbilt, paid for the study. It uses 2023-24 data, leaves out Vanderbilt University Medical Center, and assumes 55% of alumni stay in Tennessee and work 30-year careers. Statewide, the association’s schools generate more than [$22 billion a year and support 135,490 jobs](https://email.editor.thetennesseeflyover.com/c/eJyk0DluwzAQheHTUJ0FDqnFLFikUee0KYUROZQGoRaIExm5fWBfIRf48N7_9RgfyJm3-RNX8iJp3OhZMonQOSb8JlqR84VbpHPiLIXCvu2j0aa7Adw0jBiELxobrKKfDDhsQkUeemdbC9bcq8WbaUohtt3dJOsaiiH2rtUT9LqzDhNU7F8ggAYAfW_6uidwbde1ZENyDqNqNEWW_axlIaFto1KIUv7dLzrrsK9V9ovIUZT9UGZQZhAOP1jv56zMcOBMygzv6SsHXg8MUp0-Hk_OmUvXq0bPr6NvSv7Z4fLmLwAA__9txHLO), plus more than $695 million in state and local sales and property taxes. Vanderbilt alone accounts for $169 million in state and local tax impact.

Dear Patriot, Right now, in campaign offices across this country, people are looking at the new volunteer a little differently, and [**that's exactly why I need you with me**](https://email.alert.republicantaskforce.com/c/eJyckT-vnDAQxD-N6Th5d_lzFC4ina57aVOixV7AejZGxrxTvn3EJSnSptyZ2ZF-mh8f4wf74LflO0cxucxjPkZfUnBllejji4td_bb00GitR9TY1QC1hpFt8V8yNlw546xjsJUY6AdqCTukajXUO4d3BHbgoBfbNuxsO91xoOE-d_fKm6sPQAMAaYTb4ICGdhqYyDV9h6rRHCSXW5b9nIK3vBU-PueUrdxsilUwayn7oeibwqfC5yH2zHLjTVwqV0LhM32KzBLFeV5yOvdLikst4eCf4uq2jlO9p50VPc8SxyOd2Yqixz8hhd1lXi1nVPR4P_zWLMed_bIpevzBwb9O2opsRdEjl1lhxzGd75PaKhu3v3wI_uh61eglsg9vpPKfK3wZ_BUAAP__VKOWmg). Two weeks ago, I posted a warning to every midterm campaign in America: "We have undercover people inside midterm campaigns across the United States." And I told them: | "I'm watching every single thing you ALL are doing."
---
714,000 people saw that post. The campaigns saw it too. Then Detroit came out, and a man who swore he could spot one of us from across the room learned that he had been talking to one of my journalists all along.
So what's on the other tapes? **I can't tell you yet,** and I want you to understand exactly why, because the reason is the same thing that made Detroit hold up the moment it went public.
I said in that same post that we would not release footage until we had checked the facts, corroborated our sources and gotten comment, so that every story was **absolutely bulletproof.** That promise is the most expensive part of what we do. It means editors reviewing every hour of raw footage, researchers checking every claim against the public record, and calls to every person on tape to give them a chance to explain. Then the lawyers read every word. [**Help me keep that promise.**](https://email.alert.republicantaskforce.com/c/eJyckT-vnDAQxD-N6Th5d_lzFC4ina57aVOixV7AejZGxrxTvn3EJSnSptyZ2ZF-mh8f4wf74LflO0cxucxjPkZfUnBllejji4td_bb00GitR9TY1QC1hpFt8V8yNlw546xjsJUY6AdqCTukajXUO4d3BHbgoBfbNuxsO91xoOE-d_fKm6sPQAMAaYTb4ICGdhqYyDV9h6rRHCSXW5b9nIK3vBU-PueUrdxsilUwayn7oeibwqfC5yH2zHLjTVwqV0LhM32KzBLFeV5yOvdLikst4eCf4uq2jlO9p50VPc8SxyOd2Yqixz8hhd1lXi1nVPR4P_zWLMed_bIpevzBwb9O2opsRdEjl1lhxzGd75PaKhu3v3wI_uh61eglsg9vpPKfK3wZ_BUAAP__VKOWmg)
[](https://email.alert.republicantaskforce.com/c/eJyckT-vnDAQxD-N6Th5d_lzFC4ina57aVOixV7AejZGxrxTvn3EJSnSptyZ2ZF-mh8f4wf74LflO0cxucxjPkZfUnBllejji4td_bb00GitR9TY1QC1hpFt8V8yNlw546xjsJUY6AdqCTukajXUO4d3BHbgoBfbNuxsO91xoOE-d_fKm6sPQAMAaYTb4ICGdhqYyDV9h6rRHCSXW5b9nIK3vBU-PueUrdxsilUwayn7oeibwqfC5yH2zHLjTVwqV0LhM32KzBLFeV5yOvdLikst4eCf4uq2jlO9p50VPc8SxyOd2Yqixz8hhd1lXi1nVPR4P_zWLMed_bIpevzBwb9O2opsRdEjl1lhxzGd75PaKhu3v3wI_uh61eglsg9vpPKfK3wZ_BUAAP__VKOWmg)
It also means I won't rush. If a story is ready before Tuesday, you'll see it. If it needs one more source, it waits. I would rather be right than first, because when the denials come, and they always come, our story has to be the one still standing. Detroit showed what happens when we do it right: a campaign statement, a party statement and a staffer who is no longer employed. The next one will be held to the same standard. [**Help me get it out the door.**](https://email.alert.republicantaskforce.com/c/eJyckT-vnDAQxD-N6Th5d_lzFC4ina57aVOixV7AejZGxrxTvn3EJSnSptyZ2ZF-mh8f4wf74LflO0cxucxjPkZfUnBllejji4td_bb00GitR9TY1QC1hpFt8V8yNlw546xjsJUY6AdqCTukajXUO4d3BHbgoBfbNuxsO91xoOE-d_fKm6sPQAMAaYTb4ICGdhqYyDV9h6rRHCSXW5b9nIK3vBU-PueUrdxsilUwayn7oeibwqfC5yH2zHLjTVwqV0LhM32KzBLFeV5yOvdLikst4eCf4uq2jlO9p50VPc8SxyOd2Yqixz8hhd1lXi1nVPR4P_zWLMed_bIpevzBwb9O2opsRdEjl1lhxzGd75PaKhu3v3wI_uh61eglsg9vpPKfK3wZ_BUAAP__VKOWmg) Covering the $47,000 we spent on Detroit is what lets my team stay focused on the next release instead of the last bill. **We have two days left.**

clean_body: Why I don't release a tape until it's bulletproof, and what's coming next. | Dear Patriot, Right now, in campaign offices across this country, people are looking at the new volunteer a little differently, and . Two weeks ago, I posted a warning to every midterm campaign in America: "We have undercover people inside midterm campaigns across the United States." And I told them: | "I'm watching every single thing you ALL are doing." 714,000 people saw that post. The campaigns saw it too. Then Detroit came out, and a man who swore he could spot one of us from across the room learned that he had been talking to one of my journalists all along. So what's on the other tapes? I can't tell you yet, and I want you to understand exactly why, because the reason is the same thing that made Detroit hold up the moment it went public. I said in that same post that we would not release footage until we had checked the facts, corroborated our sources and gotten comment, so that every story was absolutely bulletproof. That promise is the most expensive part of what we do. It means editors reviewing every hour of raw footage, researchers checking every claim against the public record, and calls to every person on tape to give them a chance to explain. Then the lawyers read every word. It also means I won't rush. If a story is ready before Tuesday, you'll see it. If it needs one more source, it waits. I would rather be right than first, because when the denials come, and they always come, our story has to be the one still standing. Detroit showed what happens when we do it right: a campaign statement, a party statement and a staffer who is no longer employed. The next one will be held to the same standard. Covering the $47,000 we spent on Detroit is what lets my team stay focused on the next release instead of the last bill. We have two days left. You and your family deserve to know what's said behind these doors before you vote, and long after. | | | | | | Thank you for everything you do. In Truth, James O'Keefe Founder, O'Keefe Media Group P.S. Every campaign in America knows we're out there. ## U.S. Approves Missile Sales to Ukraine

**Whatever happened to Jiffy Pop?** For about two decades, the surest sign that something good was about to happen in an American kitchen was the sound of popping coming from a foil-covered pan being shaken on a burner. Jiffy Pop was a snack, a science experiment, and a babysitter all at once, until the microwave quietly put it out of work. It started in LaPorte, Indiana, where chemist Frederick Mennen took an earlier foil-pan product called E-Z Pop, gave it a sturdier handle and a better dome, and began marketing it as Jiffy Pop in 1959. By 1961, one California plant was turning out 15,000 pans a day. [You can see one of the early TV ads here.](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0LFuqzAUxvGnMVuQj01sGDxcKTdbulXthszhENwaTPEJNG9f0Vfo-n3Sb_i_3dqbDzHM9xc_keMhtTPtORIzre2SlpA_w3zPhCtxTsPk1-znvlVSmRPASULrkcNGLRS9G4gU6YIc2EaftbJgitFZX3mQEk2Nte0RmkraCi36RhrEThfBHRyABAANZ12auh68ttSRQdvpQVSS-sBpLT9SmHmkIT7TRmuJaSqiG5mXLPQ_oa5CXfd9L5_pwY-Ojv9YPOMo9HUT-vK-N1X3hZfX7__F6vplDzGGbKyo5H3yIf6S_LcQm1M_AQAA__98YnJ2) The jingle promised it was "as much fun to make as it is to eat," which was true, and also a dare. You held the wire handle, moved the pan in slow circles, watched the foil [swell into a silver balloon](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0LFu6yAUgOGnwVssDsTGHhjulepO6dCl3RA2h5gWGwtOgvL2VfoKnX_pG_6Pi7nYEMN-fbMbavLJ7FhLRCLM5khHKN9hvxZcMlJJfrO52N0ZwUV_AjhxMHahcEcDjdMeUaBsUIMaZSeFgr5ZtZPeq3FcFHfziELKcUDoQPBudBKGuQn6yQFwAJDQybYfBm-lwhn7Rc3SszNHFyjl9iuFnVb08ZHumNslbU3UK9FRmPzHxMTEVGttH-lGtxmfnYmprClTYWI67dPy_vny37zWJmt31BBjKL1iZ37dbIi_Hv3twl2LnwAAAP__FH1xcQ) the size of a basketball, and listened for the moment the popping slowed. Somebody always scorched it. Somebody always ate it anyway. The end came from just a few feet away on the countertop. Orville Redenbacher rolled out shelf-stable microwave popcorn in 1983, and the category exploded from $53 million in sales that year to $250 million by 1987. Three minutes and no shaking beat five minutes and a hot handle. Jiffy Pop never actually died, though. Conagra still owns it, still makes it in [one flavor, butter](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLGOoCAYhJ8GO4w_KGhBcY3dXnulQfhR9hAIsJp9-4v3Ctt-k0xmvj8f24f2wcfjt75QNZe2iE8N2BqWLafs618fj4qmYKvJXbpUHe3GBiYoAB1g06b5GzforHKIDHmHCuTCJ84kiO5UYlqWcZ9AmEWO0nLuJinsPEmzjyj2ufPqrQMYAIDDxHsxz05ziTsKI3fuyDig9S2V_jP52E504TvdWHqTri6os7VcCf9F2ErY-jxPf-L-ZoStuST7ZRq12LQPhK2f3rlvmlOm-9d7krqg71TQvsykEmlt6caW8guyjwfNOhK2wsSBia4omx8fgq9CknE4Lu3D_x3tZ_Zuxf4FAAD__1-Yhf4), and still sells it for about $2.50 a pan, usually on the bottom shelf near the microwave bags. Campers swear by it. So do fans of the 1996 opening scene in _Scream_ , where a pan burning on the stove became one of horror's great nervous-stomach props. It lost the convenience war decades ago. It is still, pop for pop, one of the best shows in the kitchen. _Did you pop Jiffy Pop back in the day? Let us know your thoughts by replying to this email._

For about two decades, the surest sign that something good was about to happen in an American kitchen was the sound of popping coming from a foil-covered pan being shaken on a burner. Jiffy Pop was a snack, a science experiment, and a babysitter all at once, until the microwave quietly put it out of work. It started in LaPorte, Indiana, where chemist Frederick Mennen took an earlier foil-pan product called E-Z Pop, gave it a sturdier handle and a better dome, and began marketing it as Jiffy Pop in 1959. By 1961, one California plant was turning out 15,000 pans a day. The jingle promised it was "as much fun to make as it is to eat," which was true, and also a dare. You held the wire handle, moved the pan in slow circles, watched the foil the size of a basketball, and listened for the moment the popping slowed. Somebody always scorched it. Somebody always ate it anyway. The end came from just a few feet away on the countertop. Orville Redenbacher rolled out shelf-stable microwave popcorn in 1983, and the category exploded from $53 million in sales that year to $250 million by 1987. Three minutes and no shaking beat five minutes and a hot handle. Jiffy Pop never actually died, though. Conagra still owns it, still makes it in , and still sells it for about $2.50 a pan, usually on the bottom shelf near the microwave bags. Campers swear by it. So do fans of the 1996 opening scene in Scream , where a pan burning on the stove became one of horror's great nervous-stomach props. It lost the convenience war decades ago. It is still, pop for pop, one of the best shows in the kitchen. Did you pop Jiffy Pop back in the day?
