In the movie _Wall Street_ , Gordon Gekko famously declares that "greed is good." But there is another g-word that the actual Wall Street might also love, and it isn't greed. It's gridlock. Not the kind on the Long Island Expressway or on Route 93 entering Boston at rush hour. The kind in Washington where one party holds the White House and the other holds at least one chamber of Congress. For most of the last century, that has been the market's preferred form of government. And it may be about to get it once again.
With two days to go until the midterms, prediction markets on Kalshi and Polymarket give Democrats roughly a 90% or better chance of taking the House and something in the mid-to-high 60s for the Senate. The single most likely outcome priced by both markets is a full Democratic sweep of Congress, at around 70% at the time of this writing. (_See below for real time updates on the current prediction market percentages_.) If that holds, the Trump administration goes from unified control to divided government for the first time, and investors betting on legislative paralysis will be grinning.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/8bcc8e47-3c77-419e-93f0-aa5698247dab?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Why? Because a divided government seems to suggest higher returns. Ned Davis Research tracked returns of the Dow Jones Index by government configuration going back to 1901. Divided governments, where at least one chamber of Congress is held by the opposing party, returned an annualized 8.0%. Unified governments returned 4.0%. _Double!_
When you break it down further, the picture gets more interesting. Unified Republican government, like we have had for the past two years, is the worst of all four possibilities, at just 1.54% annualized. A Republican president with a Democratic Congress? 6.37%, more than four times the return. The best configuration of all is a Democratic president checked by a Republican Congress, at 9.60%. The market doesn't love any particular party. It loves the restraint that comes when neither party can do whatever it wants.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/87ac0593-f81e-4ba4-a15d-82f920ad3a89?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
To be fair, there are numerous interpretations. This is far from a settled science. A pair of Oxford economists sliced the data differently, using data from 1927 to 2017 and found the opposite: unified governments have produced higher stock returns and faster growth. Average the whole century and the two camps roughly cancel out, which might by itself be the point. Over the long sweep, party control explains far less about markets than investors assume. **What matters is the starting point, and the starting point today is a unified government that has been pulling hard on every lever at once.**
[](https://substack.com/redirect/24b05291-3dca-4cbc-ae88-ad600e31a0ab?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
So how do unified and divided governments differ with respect to key economic indicators like growth and inequality?
On**growth** , there doesn't seem to be much difference. Kevin Hassett, now a senior Trump economic adviser, ran the numbers back in 2010 and found that since 1970, median real GDP growth was 3.3% in years of divided government versus 3.0% under one-party rule, with median unemployment of 5.7% versus 6.1%. On the margin, divided government outperforms, albeit only slightly. Wall Street compounded the small difference into larger financial market differences. The S&P 500 rose a median 13.5% a year under divided government against 9% when one party ruled.
One consistent finding that is quite powerful, however, is that divided governments slow the growth of federal spending. Turns out the government shrinks as a share of GDP only when control is split, and that division is a necessary, if not sufficient, condition for fiscal restraint. The three balanced budgets of the late 1990s were produced by a Democratic president and a Republican Congress that could agree on little else. And given today's runaway debt and ballooning deficits, this really matters.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/00e2e211-6966-40b9-ad08-095b043f2fb7?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
So when I summarize the evidence as I read it, it seems the economy grows marginally faster under a divided government and, perhaps more importantly, doesn't whipsaw as much. Uncertainty falls. When a unified government can plausibly rewrite trade policy, tax policy and industrial policy in a single session, every capital-spending decision bears an uncertainty premium. Remove the possibility of rapid sweeping change and that premium collapses. Businesses don't need Washington to help. They need to know Washington will stay out of the way and leave them alone.
When it comes to **inequality** , the data is pretty clear. Unified Democratic control in Washington pushes the top-1% share down over time; unified Republican control pushes it up. Divided government sits in between, which is to say it leaves the distribution roughly where it was prior to the divided government getting sworn in.
The implication is that divided government is a hedge against redistribution risk in both directions. The past two years delivered tax cuts whose benefits flowed disproportionately to capital, alongside tariffs that function as a regressive consumption tax on labor and everyone else. A Democratic Congress cannot reverse either without the president's signature. But it can block the next round.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/ece09dbb-fdfa-441c-8f96-09f208dcfb2d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
The common belief that divided government means nothing gets done isn't quite accurate. It's probably better to say nothing _overtly partisan_ gets done, but what does get done is usually consequential. Consider what has gotten done during divided governments over the last 50 years. The 1983 Social Security rescue, negotiated by Ronald Reagan and Tip O'Neill. The 1986 Tax Reform Act, the last time Washington actually simplified the code. The 1990 Clean Air Act amendments and the Americans with Disabilities Act. Welfare reform in 1996 and the Balanced Budget Act of 1997. The 2015 highway bill and the 2018 criminal justice reform.
Interestingly, none of this legislation was anyone's first choice. All of them stuck, because legislation that needs both parties to pass tends to survive the next election, whereas legislation passed on a party-line vote gets re-litigated the moment the majority flips.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..qIqrH58m5QbF107JDZQGDHKVJ8qLUpBO8JcA1FhI96w?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=222957196)
So on the margin, the gridlock of divided government is probably good, right? Maybe. It depends. As I noted above, the starting point matters. So let's look at where we stand after two years of a unified government:
* Tariffs that the Tax Foundation estimates cost the average household roughly $1,000 last year and another $820 this year, with the New York Fed finding that businesses and consumers absorbed nearly 90% of the burden.
* Diesel at $6.35 a gallon as of the Energy Department's latest weekly survey, a record and up $2.63 from a year ago. A war with Iran that has kept the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed to commercial traffic for more than 240 days, with Brent at $113.
* A Federal Reserve that held rates at 3.75% to 4% this week and could not cut, with two officials dissenting in favor of a hike because inflation won't cooperate.
* A 10-year Treasury that touched 5.2% earlier this month, a level unseen since 2007, and a 30-year still above 5.3%.
* And a stock market so stretched that the Buffett Indicator, total market capitalization to GDP, sits somewhere between 233% and 244% depending on who is counting, the highest ever recorded. At the dot-com peak it was roughly 140%. We are _way above_ the previous bubble.

A Democratic Congress can't really fix any of this, at least not quickly. It won't bring diesel back to $3 or immediately end the war. But it can do something important: it can stop making things worse. No new tariffs. No more blank-check spending on AI subsidies or military adventures. No active industrial policy that crowns national champions. In the current environment, the most bullish thing Washington can do is nothing.
Bloomberg Intelligence's Mike McGlone recently drew a scary parallel to the Hoover era: Market cap at about 2.5 times GDP, commodities surging, a Federal Reserve tightening into what may be the late innings of a cycle.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/e1b1848f-62a3-41e4-924f-35248ad664cb?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
It is the kind of comparison nobody wants to make, and everybody should. _It 's probably prudent to ask: Are we headed into a Depression? And if so, will that create a unification of purpose, even among a divided government?_
Some will say divided government means no progress on deficit reduction, no structural reform, just two years of posturing before 2028. That may be true. _**But we are past the point where Washington needs to do something. We are at the point where it needs to stop doing things**_. Stop pouring fiscal gasoline on an inflationary fire. Stop starting trade wars. Stop starting real wars. The market doesn't need leadership from Washington right now. It needs a breather.
* * *
## [The Canary in the Frozen Food Aisle](https://substack.com/redirect/dde8fb15-ab63-4ca1-ab0d-d7726385f422?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)

Frozen pizza isn't a product. It's a signal. And right now, the signal is flashing red.](https://substack.com/redirect/dde8fb15-ab63-4ca1-ab0d-d7726385f422?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)

* * *
I keep coming back to a line from the late MIT economist Rudiger Dornbusch: in economics, things take longer to happen than you think they will, and then they happen faster than you thought they could. The Buffett Indicator above 230%. Diesel at records. Bitcoin at $77,000, nearly 40% below its peak. Gold down 27% from its January high, and yet long Treasuries still yielding more than 5%. These are not signs of stability.
Readers know that the core theme of my work is how to navigate uncertainty. Unified governments create a lot of it, because they can act unilaterally and do many things whose ramifications they can barely fathom. That makes navigation more challenging. Divided governments find little they can agree on and little they can actually get done...which suggests whatever does get done is well-vetted, important, and usually durable.
While it's impossible to know if we're heading towards a more certain environment, Tuesday's midterm results will definitely shed some light on how the next two years will feel.

Why Wall Street might be rooting for a divided Washington on November 3rd. | | | Nov 1 | | | | | | | | | | | | | | ---|---|--- In the movie Wall Street , Gordon Gekko famously declares that "greed is good." But there is another g-word that the actual Wall Street might also love, and it isn't greed. It's gridlock. Not the kind on the Long Island Expressway or on Route 93 entering Boston at rush hour. The kind in Washington where one party holds the White House and the other holds at least one chamber of Congress. For most of the last century, that has been the market's preferred form of government. And it may be about to get it once again. With two days to go until the midterms, prediction markets on Kalshi and Polymarket give Democrats roughly a 90% or better chance of taking the House and something in the mid-to-high 60s for the Senate. The single most likely outcome priced by both markets is a full Democratic sweep of Congress, at around 70% at the time of this writing. (See below for real time updates on the current prediction market percentages.) If that holds, the Trump administration goes from unified control to divided government for the first time, and investors betting on legislative paralysis will be grinning. Why? Because a divided government seems to suggest higher returns. Ned Davis Research tracked returns of the Dow Jones Index by government configuration going back to 1901. Divided governments, where at least one chamber of Congress is held by the opposing party, returned an annualized 8.0%. Unified governments returned 4.0%. Double! When you break it down further, the picture gets more interesting. Unified Republican government, like we have had for the past two years, is the worst of all four possibilities, at just 1.54% annualized. A Republican president with a Democratic Congress? 6.37%, more than four times the return. The best configuration of all is a Democratic president checked by a Republican Congress, at 9.60%. The market doesn't love any particular party. It loves the restraint that comes when neither party can do whatever it wants. To be fair, there are numerous interpretations. This is far from a settled science. A pair of Oxford economists sliced the data differently, using data from 1927 to 2017 and found the opposite: unified governments have produced higher stock returns and faster growth. Average the whole century and the two camps roughly cancel out, which might by itself be the point. Over the long sweep, party control explains far less about markets than investors assume. What matters is the starting point, and the starting point today is a unified government that has been pulling hard on every lever at once. So how do unified and divided governments differ with respect to key economic indicators like growth and inequality? Ongrowth , there doesn't seem to be much difference. Kevin Hassett, now a senior Trump economic adviser, ran the numbers back in 2010 and found that since 1970, median real GDP growth was 3.3% in years of divided government versus 3.0% under one-party rule, with median unemployment of 5.7% versus 6.1%. On the margin, divided government outperforms, albeit only slightly. Wall Street compounded the small difference into larger financial market differences. The S&P 500 rose a median 13.5% a year under divided government against 9% when one party ruled. One consistent finding that is quite powerful, however, is that divided governments slow the growth of federal spending. Turns out the government shrinks as a share of GDP only when control is split, and that division is a necessary, if not sufficient, condition for fiscal restraint. The three balanced budgets of the late 1990s were produced by a Democratic president and a Republican Congress that could agree on little else. And given today's runaway debt and ballooning deficits, this really matters. So when I summarize the evidence as I read it, it seems the economy grows marginally faster under a divided government and, perhaps more importantly, doesn't whipsaw as much. Uncertainty falls. When a unified government can plausibly rewrite trade policy, tax policy and industrial policy in a single session, every capital-spending decision bears an uncertainty premium. Remove the possibility of rapid sweeping change and that premium collapses. Businesses don't need Washington to help. They need to know Washington will stay out of the way and leave them alone. When it comes to inequality , the data is pretty clear. Unified Democratic control in Washington pushes the top-1% share down over time; unified Republican control pushes it up. Divided government sits in between, which is to say it leaves the distribution roughly where it was prior to the divided government getting sworn in. The implication is that divided government is a hedge against redistribution risk in both directions. The past two years delivered tax cuts whose benefits flowed disproportionately to capital, alongside tariffs that function as a regressive consumption tax on labor and everyone else. A Democratic Congress cannot reverse either without the president's signature. But it can block the next round. The common belief that divided government means nothing gets done isn't quite accurate. It's probably better to say nothing overtly partisan gets done, but what does get done is usually consequential. Consider what has gotten done during divided governments over the last 50 years. The 1983 Social Security rescue, negotiated by Ronald Reagan and Tip O'Neill. The 1986 Tax Reform Act, the last time Washington actually simplified the code. The 1990 Clean Air Act amendments and the Americans with Disabilities Act. Welfare reform in 1996 and the Balanced Budget Act of 1997. The 2015 highway bill and the 2018 criminal justice reform. Interestingly, none of this legislation was anyone's first choice. All of them stuck, because legislation that needs both parties to pass tends to survive the next election, whereas legislation passed on a party-line vote gets re-litigated the moment the majority flips. So on the margin, the gridlock of divided government is probably good, right? Maybe. It depends. As I noted above, the starting point matters. So let's look at where we stand after two years of a unified government: Tariffs that the Tax Foundation estimates cost the average household roughly $1,000 last year and another $820 this year, with the New York Fed finding that businesses and consumers absorbed nearly 90% of the burden. Diesel at $6.35 a gallon as of the Energy Department's latest weekly survey, a record and up $2.63 from a year ago. A war with Iran that has kept the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed to commercial traffic for more than 240 days, with Brent at $113. A Federal Reserve that held rates at 3.75% to 4% this week and could not cut, with two officials dissenting in favor of a hike because inflation won't cooperate. A 10-year Treasury that touched 5.2% earlier this month, a level unseen since 2007, and a 30-year still above 5.3%. And a stock market so stretched that the Buffett Indicator, total market capitalization to GDP, sits somewhere between 233% and 244% depending on who is counting, the highest ever recorded. At the dot-com peak it was roughly 140%. We are way above the previous bubble. A Democratic Congress can't really fix any of this, at least not quickly. It won't bring diesel back to $3 or immediately end the war. But it can do something important: it can stop making things worse. No new tariffs. No more blank-check spending on AI subsidies or military adventures. No active industrial policy that crowns national champions. In the current environment, the most bullish thing Washington can do is nothing. Bloomberg Intelligence's Mike McGlone recently drew a scary parallel to the Hoover era: Market cap at about 2.5 times GDP, commodities surging, a Federal Reserve tightening into what may be the late innings of a cycle. It is the kind of comparison nobody wants to make, and everybody should. It 's probably prudent to ask: Are we headed into a Depression? And if so, will that create a unification of purpose, even among a divided government? Some will say divided government means no progress on deficit reduction, no structural reform, just two years of posturing before 2028. That may be true. But we are past the point where Washington needs to do something. We are at the point where it needs to stop doing things. Stop pouring fiscal gasoline on an inflationary fire. Stop starting trade wars. Stop starting real wars. The market doesn't need leadership from Washington right now. It needs a breather. | | | | ---|---|--- | Oct 11 | I keep coming back to a line from the late MIT economist Rudiger Dornbusch: in economics, things take longer to happen than you think they will, and then they happen faster than you thought they could. The Buffett Indicator above 230%. Diesel at records. Bitcoin at $77,000, nearly 40% below its peak. Gold down 27% from its January high, and yet long Treasuries still yielding more than 5%. These are not signs of stability. Readers know that the core theme of my work is how to navigate uncertainty. Unified governments create a lot of it, because they can act unilaterally and do many things whose ramifications they can barely fathom. That makes navigation more challenging. Divided governments find little they can agree on and little they can actually get done...which suggests whatever does get done is well-vetted, important, and usually durable. While it's impossible to know if we're heading towards a more certain environment, Tuesday's midterm results will definitely shed some light on how the next two years will feel. | | ---|---|--- VIKRAM MANSHARAMANI is an entrepreneur, consultant, scholar, neighbor, husband, father, volunteer, and professional generalist who thinks in multiple-dimensions and looks beyond the short-term. name: Sen. Jeff Bridges
subject: Mayor Pete's first campaign wasn't for president
body:
Pete Buttigieg told a packed room how hard it is to get people excited about a State Treasurer's race. He would know. He ran for Indiana Treasurer

| | | | | | | [View this email in your browser](https://mailchi.mp/4b7f424d0f73/get-more-smarter-on-colorados-budget-10379931?e=b48bb2b4f4)
---
[|
---](https://us.list-manage.com/SZth39NoFq_?e=b48bb2b4f4&c2id=bbe572662fdb5fed2d0855c1bcb00da8)
| | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | Hi there,
On Wednesday in Highlands Ranch, Pete Buttigieg told a packed room how hard it is to get people excited about a State Treasurer's race. He would know. He ran for Indiana State Treasurer in 2010.
**I shouted back, "The most important office in the state!" Everyone laughed. I was only kind of joking.**
Congressman Joe Neguse, who grew up in Highlands Ranch, joined us alongside longtime Douglas County Democrats. Having grown up in Arapahoe County, I know what it’s like when red counties turn blue. This is their year.
---
[|
---](https://us.list-manage.com/Tk5CzSX1kPX?e=b48bb2b4f4&c2id=bbe572662fdb5fed2d0855c1bcb00da8)
| | Nobody talks about faith and governing better than Pete.
I've long believed a budget is a moral document. It puts in dollars and cents exactly what we value and how much. The same goes for our investments, because where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
**That's why the Treasurer's office matters. We can put Colorado dollars to work in Colorado to build homes people can afford, renewable energy that lowers bills, and child care that doesn't cost more than rent.**
Pete told me he appreciated how I explained why the Treasurer's office matters. He'd struggled with that when he ran. I told him things seem to have worked out pretty well for him all the same.
---
[|
---](https://us.list-manage.com/s6yBLqa9Fe2?e=b48bb2b4f4&c2id=bbe572662fdb5fed2d0855c1bcb00da8)
| | It's too late to mail your ballot! Use an official drop box or voting center by 7 p.m. Tuesday, November 3.
[Find your nearest ballot drop box here.](https://us.list-manage.com/6FA89VYQjwH?e=b48bb2b4f4&c2id=bbe572662fdb5fed2d0855c1bcb00da8) And if you’ve already voted, make sure your friends and family vote, too!
Talk soon,
ps We lost Captain Picard this week. Pete is a huge Star Trek nerd, and when he guest-hosted _Jimmy Kimmel_ , he interviewed Sir Patrick Stewart, who surprised him with an original Star Trek script. [It's worth a watch.](https://us.list-manage.com/7s1vT_HZykr?e=b48bb2b4f4&c2id=bbe572662fdb5fed2d0855c1bcb00da8) Godspeed, Captain.
---

Friend, we know we’ve been reaching out a lot, but there’s a reason we’re asking again today. We’re at a point in this race where we are making tough decisions that have a real impact on what we’re able to do in the days ahead. _Let us explain:_
**1.** The latest poll shows Deb’s race is**closer than anyone expected.
****
2.** Republicans see this race as a **top pickup opportunity,** especially knowing New Mexico’s governorship tends to flip parties every eight years.

**3.** Deb’s Republican opponent is bankrolled by many of Trump’s TOP supporters in New Mexico and is focused on bringing Trump’s extremism to New Mexico.
Between now and Election Day, keeping our ads on TV, traveling across New Mexico, organizing events, and reaching voters takes real resources. **And the closer we get to Election Day, the more quickly those decisions and investments have to be made.** _None of us want to look back the morning after Election Day wishing we’d done a little more. Because the stakes couldn’t be higher — for our working families, our public lands, and our kids’ and grandkids’ futures._
That’s why you’re hearing from us again — because what happens right now will shape what we’re able to do in the final stretch. subject: Donald Trump just attacked me by name
disclaimer_text: Paid for by the Committee to Elect Enoch, Catherine Johnson, Treasurer
body:
I never expected to wake up to the President of the United States writing about me.

| | | | | |
---
| | | | [|
---](https://us.list-manage.com/3LyMDMrenOg?e=c6e7dff14c&c2id=d95570268fc9105c688a303b4f3b91b8)
| [RSVP](https://us.list-manage.com/ATmUKVgM1xl?e=c6e7dff14c&c2id=d95570268fc9105c688a303b4f3b91b8)
---
| | Hello Peter,
I'll be honest with you: I never expected to wake up to the President of the United States writing about me.
On Friday afternoon, Donald Trump posted a full endorsement of Warren Davidson on Truth Social, and then spent the rest of it calling me "Reckless, Radical, and Dangerous."
Here's what that tells me. Presidents don't spend their time on races they think are safe. They weigh in when they're worried. And they're worried because this campaign is gaining ground across Butler, Hamilton, Preble, and Darke counties. Neighbors are talking. Volunteers are knocking doors. People are ready for a representative who shows up for them.
Now comes the part I can't do alone. When a national figure puts a target on a campaign, money and attack ads usually follow. We need to make sure every voter in OH-08 hears the truth from us, not a caricature written in Washington.
We have just two days left. Here are two ways you can help us finish strong:GIVE: Your gift right now goes straight into our final push: get-out-the-vote calls, digital ads, and rides to the polls. Will you chip in $25, $50, or $100?

name: Kristen McDonald Rivet
subject: Our final push
body:
|
#

# **Why we are voting for Reed!**
---
|
---
| |
# “Reed is the kinda guy that shows up.”
_-Amy Karwoski_
---
| | Reed was one of the first people I met after arriving in Bemidji from NYC. Shortly after meeting at the public library, he offered me a spare AC unit for my sweltering rental. To my surprise, he returned with it a few minutes later.
Fast-forward 7 years, and we have spent 4 of them working together– as the administrative wing of the _Nameless Coalition for the Homeless_ and also as his current campaign coordinator. During this time, I have gotten to know Reed as**a leader, an advocate, a problem solver, a public servant, a visionary, a squeaky wheel, a canary in the coal mine, an empath and a loyal friend** to many.
---
| | | | | | | | | | |
---
| |
---
| | **I can attest that Reed is the kinda guy who:**
-Drives you to a doctor appt. during a busy workday-Takes care of your cat when you have to leave town-Agrees to dress up with you for Halloween so you don’t feel stupid-Calls the AG when you are fighting with your bank-Drops off homemade bone broth when you are sick-Continuously fixes your fishing pole-Encourages you to become a more informed, powerful version of yourself-Is your emergency contact because he is actually the most likely to show up
I have watched Reed advocate for hundreds of individuals over the years, as county commissioner and as non-profit director (for years without pay). He treats every person he meets like family. He brings the same kinetic energy to every problem and the same pugnacious creativity to every solution.
**I trust Reed to be my elected representative.**
I feel strongly enough about getting Reed elected that I agreed to join his campaign full-time. I have benefitted greatly from his friendship over the years and I want to live in a world where all my neighbors have a guy like him in their corner.
Reed is the kinda guy that shows up.
**He will be the representative that shows up for you.**
_Amy Karwoski_ Campaign ManagerVote Reed Olson

| | | Hi there, it's Martin Sheen. I know seeing my name in your inbox might come as a surprise, but I need to talk to you about the country we both love ‐‐ and why I hope you'll fight for it alongside me.

If you don't have time to hear my whole pitch, here's my ask: [**Will you join me in the fight for our future by donating $7 _(generously matched to $35)_ to help my friends at the DSCC take back the Senate for Democrats?**](https://go.dscc.org/go/24502?amount=7&t=5&firstname=&lastname=&email=dpwillis67%40gmail.com&addr1=&addr2=&city=Cresco&state=Pennsylvania&zip=18326&phone=None&employer=&occupation=&ask=7&amounts=7%2C14%2C28%2C70&code=DPE-FD-20261101-MartinSheen-WhatASKMeans2026RF-Pros-sl1&refcode=DPE-FD-20261101-MartinSheen-WhatASKMeans2026RF-Pros-sl1&akid=27274%2E9716520%2E6ykqz8)

You see, I was once the "acting" president of the United States ‐‐ and while I may have been playing a fictional role, the lessons I learned were very real.

I'll let you in on the most important one: **Every person has the power to make a difference.**

You might find that hard to believe right now, after everything we've seen and endured in the past two years.

I certainly wouldn't blame you for feeling that way.

But look beyond the terrible headlines, and you might just see what I see: Americans of every background and belief, standing up in ways big and small, _sacrificing_ to bring about a future better than our present.

Whether they succeed is, in part, up to you.

One seemingly small action you can take to help is to join with your fellow Democrats and pitch in $7 to help elect a Democratic Senate majority.

Flipping the Senate and bringing accountability to this administration _will_ make a difference, but it will only be possible if we lock hands, raise our voices, and come together ‐‐ that's when we can accomplish truly incredible things.

**The headwinds we face are strong, but we are stronger. Donald Trump is determined, but we are more determined. And right now, as we stretch our arms toward the future, I hope you'll join me.**

[**I'm coming to you humbly: Before the midnight deadline passes, will you contribute $7 to the DSCC as we take the next step together? Thanks to help from a kind group of donors, we're unlocking a _quintuple ‐impact match_ so your gift will go five times as far!**](https://go.dscc.org/go/24502?amount=7&t=6&firstname=&lastname=&email=dpwillis67%40gmail.com&addr1=&addr2=&city=Cresco&state=Pennsylvania&zip=18326&phone=None&employer=&occupation=&ask=7&amounts=7%2C14%2C28%2C70&code=DPE-FD-20261101-MartinSheen-WhatASKMeans2026RF-Pros-sl1&refcode=DPE-FD-20261101-MartinSheen-WhatASKMeans2026RF-Pros-sl1&akid=27274%2E9716520%2E6ykqz8)

VA-02 is one of the REAL toss-up races in America, and the decision you make today could have a massive impact this November.

Jen is a Navy Veteran who flew H-46 and H-3 helicopters and completed two deployments to the Persian Gulf. After her service, Jen became a board-certified Nurse Practitioner and continued to serve in long-term care and nursing facilities in Virginia Beach and Norfolk. Her entire life has been dedicated to service.

With the rise of the DSA and socialists, I’m extremely worried if Democrats win this seat. If they do, they will be even closer to flipping the House, and will immediately move to:

* Defund ICE
* Raise our taxes

Kellyanne Conway

name: Deb Haaland
subject: Do you believe in my vision for New Mexico? Add your name!
disclaimer_text: PAID FOR AND AUTHORIZED BY DEB FOR NEW MEXICO**
body:
| | | [](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/1101?source=jtk1709-su-nd&refcode=jtk1709-su-nd&t=1&akid=13607%2E400544%2EtJKHHI)
---
Friend: In a moment, I'm going to share with you my vision for New Mexico — **_[but first, can I ask you to take 30 seconds to personally endorse my campaign for Governor?](https://act.debhaaland.com/signup/em_mw_202611_endorse_vision?email=dpwillis67@gmail.com&zip=&ask=5&source=jtk1709-su-nd&refcode=jtk1709-su-nd&t=2&akid=13607%2E400544%2EtJKHHI)_**
| | [Add My Name](https://act.debhaaland.com/signup/em_mw_202611_endorse_vision?email=dpwillis67@gmail.com&zip=&ask=5&source=jtk1709-su-nd&refcode=jtk1709-su-nd&t=3&akid=13607%2E400544%2EtJKHHI)
---
This message is a bit on the longer side, but because you're invested in the future of New Mexico, I hope you'll take the time to read my plan. **As New Mexico’s next Governor, I will:**
**Build Education That Works for New Mexico by:**
* Ensuring students can read before third grade by identifying literacy challenges early and providing targeted support when children fall behind

* Strengthening early literacy screening, expanding bilingual and reading instruction, and investing in summer reading and after-school programs that reinforce learning beyond the school day

* Bolstering access to universal childcare, because learning begins long before a child enters a classroom

* Directing unspent dollars from the Public School Capital Outlay Fund to modernize and improve school facilities so kids can focus on learning

* Expanding outdoor and place-based learning through my Every Child Outdoor Initiative, giving schools the tools and resources to connect classroom instruction to real-world learning that improves engagement and outcomes

**Support New Mexico Families by:**
* Raising the minimum wage and eliminating predatory junk fees

* Passing Paid Family and Medical Leave so people don’t have to choose between caring for their family and making ends meet

* Increasing the child tax credit to put money back into your pockets

* Creating a statewide tenant bill of rights to make renting more affordable and more transparent

* Creating a Critical Sector Housing Fund for workers in critical sectors — like healthcare, behavioral health, social work, education, and more — to recruit more professionals to New Mexico to address endemic shortages that hold our people back

* Aggressively building more housing, eliminating unnecessary red tape, driving state investment into housing, and shortening the time it takes to build a home — and ensuring those homes are built with New Mexican labor

**Back Small Businesses by:**
* Establishing a permanent Office of Small Business to coordinate development programs, fill gaps left by federal cuts, and provide clear access to grants, capital, and state resources

* Cracking down on predatory lending by requiring full transparency in small-business loan disclosures

* Establishing a New Mexico Economic Growth Trust Fund to stabilize our economy in the face of federal uncertainty

**Fix Our Broken Healthcare System by:**
* Protecting and expanding access to healthcare in every part of New Mexico

* Banning medical debt from being included on credit reports

* Expanding New Mexico’s Health Care Affordability Fund to protect access for those who rely on the state marketplace

* Using budget surpluses to fill Medicaid gaps and hire more guides to help people enroll in and keep their benefits

* Ensuring sustainable funding for rural hospitals and clinics, expanding mobile health clinics, and significantly increasing access to outpatient behavioral and mental healthcare, including a full-scale effort to deliver mental health and homelessness assistance statewide

**Strengthen Public Safety by:**
* Ensuring that law enforcement has the tools, staffing, and technology they need to do their jobs effectively

* Investing in mental and behavioral healthcare and housing stability

* Expanding violence intervention and prevention programs in schools and communities, building accountability systems that emphasize fairness and trust, and investing in community policing models that supplement traditional police work

* Creating a statewide Department of Community Safety staffed with social workers and counselors so law enforcement can focus on violent crime while people get the help they need

* Requiring ICE agents to clearly identify themselves and prohibiting masks that shield misconduct from accountability

New Mexico deserves steady leadership that’s ready on day one, leadership rooted in firsthand knowledge and experience. But the only way we'll be able to make this vision a reality is with strong grassroots support from people like you.
**I'm aiming to get 10,000 endorsements for my campaign before my midnight deadline to show the grassroots strength behind my vision for New Mexico, and I want you to be one of them._[Will you please take a quick moment to sign on now?](https://act.debhaaland.com/signup/em_mw_202611_endorse_vision?email=dpwillis67@gmail.com&zip=&ask=5&source=jtk1709-su-nd&refcode=jtk1709-su-nd&t=4&akid=13607%2E400544%2EtJKHHI)_**
| | [Add My Name](https://act.debhaaland.com/signup/em_mw_202611_endorse_vision?email=dpwillis67@gmail.com&zip=&ask=5&source=jtk1709-su-nd&refcode=jtk1709-su-nd&t=5&akid=13607%2E400544%2EtJKHHI)
---
Thank you for your support,

Deb

First, a huge thank you to everyone who has contributed their time, energy, and resources to the Bradstock campaign. Whether you've knocked on doors, made phone calls, attended town halls, donated, or volunteered in countless other ways, your efforts have made this campaign possible. As Election Day approaches, please remind your friends, family, and neighbors that polls will be open Tuesday from 7 AM to 8 PM. Make sure they know where to vote and have the information they need to participate. name: James Talarico
subject: A political earthquake
body:
[1]Talarico for Texas

Hey Peter, it's James Talarico. I want to say upfront
how grateful I am that you are part of this movement.

We’re in the final hours of this race, and so many folks are
pouring their time and treasure into making sure we win. We’re on
the cusp of not just making history here in Texas — but
fundamentally changing American politics. Our victory would send
a political earthquake across this country.
[2]James
Right now, the polls mean nothing. We know we can win, but just Talarico
one fumble is all it takes to lose, too. Millions of Texans still
need to vote, so the only thing that matters is that we don’t
take anything for granted or let off the gas.

It’s not over until every ballot is counted. I’m leaving it all
on the field, but I can’t do it alone. [ https://act.jamestalarico.com/go/512?c0=jt-em-2026q4.erR9_P&refcode=em261101-2-ak&t=1001&akid=1185%2E1347274%2EaEUfFa ]So please, I’m
personally asking you to click this link and donate to help us
take back Texas. No corporate PAC money. Just people power. James
Talarico

[ https://act.jamestalarico.com/go/512?c0=jt-em-2026q4.erR9_P&refcode=em261101-2-ak&t=1002&akid=1185%2E1347274%2EaEUfFa ]CONTRIBUTE

[ https://act.jamestalarico.com/go/512?c0=jt-em-2026q4.erR9_P&refcode=em261101-2-ak&t=1003&akid=1185%2E1347274%2EaEUfFa ]'New York Times: In Texas, Talarico Inspires a Recurring Blue-Tinted
Dream In the go-big-or-go-home collective consciousness of Texas, no
ambition is deemed too reckless, no daydream too wild. Save perhaps one.
It is the idea, fantastical to many as it is irresistible to others, that
the Democrats will win a statewide race in Texas for the first time in 32
years. According to the latest New York Times/Siena University poll of the
race for U.S. Senate, James Talarico, a 37-year-old state legislator seen
by national Democrats as one of the breakout stars of this cycle, is ahead
of his Republican rival, Ken Paxton, the state’s scandal-plagued attorney
general, by six points. The poll was conducted from Sept. 21 to Sept. 30.
A survey from mid-September, the ReconMR/Siena Research Institute poll,
also showed the Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Gina Hinojosa, four
points ahead of the three-term G.O.P. incumbent, Greg Abbott, the most
dominant political figure in Texas. Cue the fluttering heartbeats. Cue, as
well, the eye-rolls. Given how thoroughly Republicans have dominated the
state, and how the hopes of Democrats have repeatedly crashed, some Texas
pollsters remain skeptical. “At some point, you do get conditioned by all
that’s happened in the past,” said James Henson, the director of the
University of Texas at Austin’s Texas Politics Project. “I mean, you look
at the trends and you have to admit that something’s going on. But you
still don’t want to believe your lying eyes, because you’ve been burned
for so long.” Mr. Henson was referring to the perennial spectacle of
much-ballyhooed Texas Democratic aspirants face-planting against the Lone
Star State’s red wall. First came Tony Sanchez Jr., the swaggering and
self-funding Laredo oilman whom Gov. Rick Perry dispatched in 2002 by an
18-point margin. Next was the state senator Wendy Davis, who attracted
worldwide attention for her filibuster in the Texas Legislature against an
anti-abortion measure but whom Mr. Abbott demolished by 20 points in 2014.
Finally, the El Paso congressman Beto O’Rourke came up 2.6 points short of
defeating Senator Ted Cruz in 2018 but then suffered a 10-point loss to
Mr. Abbott four years later. Even with the awareness of such humiliations,
Democrats find themselves maintaining that 2026 could, at long last, be
the year. President Trump’s deep unpopularity and the prospect of a blue
wave could, they insist, extend into the state he won by nearly 14 points
in 2024. According to a September survey conducted by Texas Southern
University, Mr. Trump is seven points underwater in Texas. Mr. Talarico
has run an energetic and well-financed campaign, while Mr. Paxton has
staged far fewer public events and has had to rely on outside groups to
fund an attack-ad blitzkrieg against his Democratic opponent. Mr. Abbott,
meanwhile, has outspent Ms. Hinojosa by a 10-to-one ratio, yet has been
unable to build an insurmountable lead. “People have vastly underestimated
Gina,” said Ms. Davis, now a political consultant and a senior adviser to
Planned Parenthood Texas Votes, an advocacy organization. “Dollar for
dollar, she’s running the best statewide campaign we’ve ever seen.” Such
optimism stands in defiance of the political axiom that Texas is where
idealistic Democrats go to be mugged by reality. The party’s demise there
is not a product of ill fortune, Mr. Henson said. “Governor Abbott has
built an impressive election machine that has benefited state-level
Republicans again and again for a decade and a half,” he said. “And the
Democratic machinery here is almost nonexistent.” A ‘Hollowing-Out’ I have
written about the politics of my native state at regular intervals for
more than three decades. After watching the Democrats’ century-long rule
in Texas come to a decisive end with Gov. Ann Richards’s loss to George W.
Bush in 1994, I saw the party descend into atrophy in which failure begot
more failure. “The 30-year drought has done a lot of things,” said Luke
Warford, the chairman of the Travis County Democratic Party and the
founder of the Agave Democratic Infrastructure Fund. “It’s kept donors on
the sidelines, which makes a lot of potentially good candidates not run
because there’s no belief they can win. And it also makes a lot of really
talented staff leave to find better-paying work in true battleground
states.” The Democratic Party has no counterpart to Mr. Abbott, and hasn’t
since 1993, when Senator Lloyd Bentsen moved to Washington to join
President Bill Clinton’s cabinet. Its weaknesses are even more glaring
farther down the hierarchy. In recent elections, as many as one-third of
state races have gone uncontested by Democrats. One-fifth of the party’s
county chairs and two-thirds of its precinct chairs have been left
unfilled. Until last year, the state party had a negative operating
budget. As the veteran Democratic consultant Matt Angle observed, “There’s
been a hollowing-out of the party.” Still, those of us who recall the
satisfied sense of invincibility among Texas Democrats after roughly a
century of one-party rule have detected similar signs of overconfidence
among the state’s ruling party. The party’s rightward tilt, increasingly
forceful with each legislative session, reached its apotheosis in March,
with Mr. Paxton’s primary victory over the more moderate Republican
four-term incumbent, Senator John Cornyn. Mr. Paxton, a close ally of Mr.
Trump’s, was impeached by the Republican-controlled State House (and later
acquitted by the State Senate) in 2023 over allegations that included
bribery. He was also accused by his wife of adultery. Mr. Trump endorsed
him anyway, all but guaranteeing his landslide primary triumph over Mr.
Cornyn but in the process testing the allegiance of center-right Texans.
In similar fashion, the Texas G.O.P. is in danger of losing many Latino
voters who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 after years of siding with
Democrats. “We adopted a lazy way of campaigning that bit us on the ass,
and we’ve learned from that,” Mr. O’Rourke said. “Now it’s the Republicans
who’ve gotten really lazy and complacent and comfortable.” Signs of
Republican Overreach Simply spending one week driving through the vastness
of Texas, as I did in September, is all it takes to appreciate an underdog
party’s uphill battle. The state’s 32 million residents are spread across
20 media markets, many of them distinct ecosystems, from the urban colossi
of Houston and the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex to the oil patch of the
Texas Panhandle to the Latino-dominated borderlands of the Rio Grande
Valley. “When national donors are deciding where to invest, they look at a
place like Iowa, where $5 million can fully fund a race,” said Katherine
Fischer, the director of the Texas Majority PAC, which was established by
the liberal philanthropist Soros family. “That’s why Texas is always at
the bottom of their list. It’s just so damned big.” Reaching so many
markets presents a daunting challenge for an upstart candidate like Ms.
Hinojosa, a state representative from the border city of Brownsville.
“There’s still 20 percent of the electorate that doesn’t know who I am,”
she said in an interview in mid-September. To date, Ms. Hinojosa’s
campaign has said that it has raised about $20 million. For his part, Mr.
Talarico spent about $30 million earlier this year to introduce himself
statewide as a man of Christian faith and a member of the Texas House with
a record of supporting bipartisan legislation. Since that time, however,
Mr. Paxton and his associates have invested more than $100 million in an
effort to redefine his opponent as “radical” and “weird,” with ads that
quote from remarks Mr. Talarico made several years ago (and later
renounced) suggesting that “God is nonbinary” and that there are six
biological sexes. Mr. Paxton and his allies have at times questioned Mr.
Talarico’s manhood and even his Christianity, an effort to jolt the
sensibilities of a state prone to mythologizing godly and masculine
archetypes. “How they’re negatively defining Talarico is kind of a
bank-shot way of saying that he’s not a true Texas conservative,” Mr.
Henson said. Whether money can overwhelm conditions on the ground is the
riddle looming over the Texas races. In the border city of Laredo, which
Mr. Trump won in 2024 — the first time a Republican had done so in over a
century — signs of buyer’s remorse are evident. Arrests by Immigration and
Customs Enforcement agents in Laredo were higher in July than in any other
American city. Mr. Trump’s erratic trade policies have further created
instability at the city’s port of entry. While acknowledging the economic
concerns that many border residents share, Adrian Zapata, a business
executive in the health industry who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, said in
an interview that the negative ads against Mr. Talarico were resonating
with some of his family members. “They see Talarico as an ultraliberal,”
he said. “They’re done with the ‘they/them.’ They’re going to vote for
Paxton just because of that.” As for Mr. Zapata, “I’m not ready to vote
for Talarico,” he said. “But I don’t like Paxton. He’s never done anything
for South Texas, and his personal and business dealings have hurt him a
lot with folks down here.” There is a similarly muddled electoral picture
in the cattle country of deep West Texas adjacent to Big Bend National
Park. Mr. Trump and Mr. Abbott have aggressively championed a border wall
and artificial intelligence data centers, both of which threaten to
disrupt the region’s pastoral ethos. A coalition of more than 200
landowners has sued the federal government over the border wall, while
other residents have circulated a petition to protest the construction of
a new data center near Fort Stockton. George Johnson, a cattle feed
operator in Alpine, waved off such concerns, saying: “Folks worrying about
data centers were also worried when the internet got started. It’s
Talarico who scares me to death, him and all that socialist talk.” Others
in this largely conservative region harbor the view that Republicans have
failed to make good on their promises. Thaddeus Cleveland, the Republican
sheriff of Terrell County, said that both he and his county had voted for
Mr. Trump in 2024, but added, “Everything he campaigned on, we’re seeing
the opposite of, like going to war.” Sheriff Cleveland predicted that the
negative campaign ads by the Republicans would not factor as significantly
into the votes of his neighbors as “the price of groceries and gas, which
are compounded here because we’re so far from everywhere else.” But it is
in purple Tarrant County, dominated by Fort Worth, where the party could
pay the price for having potentially overestimated its mandate from the
voters. Conservative leaders have cut funds for nonprofits that aid
at-risk children, subjected school library books to right-wing litmus
tests and eliminated free bus rides to polling stations in poor
neighborhoods. “The far-right leaders here have implemented Project 2025
on a county level,” said Alisa Simmons, a Democrat and county commissioner
who is running to unseat the conservative county judge, Tim O’Hare. In an
early sign this year that area Republicans may be out of step with Tarrant
County’s constituents, a Democratic aviation machinist and union leader,
Taylor Rehmet, defeated Leigh Wambsganss, a well-funded Republican
Christian activist who led the conservative takeover of several metroplex
school boards. He won by 14 points in a January special election for a
State Senate seat covering a region that Mr. Trump won by 17 points in
2024. A ‘Gradualist’ Theory Which party prevails in Texas is a complicated
riddle. Historically a low-turnout state — it ranked second to last in the
2024 election, ahead of only Arkansas — Texas held a primary in March that
saw nearly one in four voters showing up to the polls, a modern record for
midterm participation, with Democrats slightly outpacing Republicans. A
few factors could conspire to thwart a blue wave in Texas. As of 2020,
straight-ticket voting is no longer possible in the state, which could
impact the mostly Democratic urban counties where that practice has
frequently been used by voters in past elections. Texas is one of only
eight states that lack universal online registration, while voting by mail
is also highly restricted. In January, Mr. Abbott turned over the state’s
list of approximately 18.7 million registered voters to the Trump
administration, and 1.2 million of them have subsequently been put on the
“suspense list” because their addresses have not been verified. The recent
shuttering of nearly one-third of Tarrant County’s polling sites by its
Republican-controlled county commission is particularly worrisome for
Democrats. “The reason we’ve lost these statewide races in the past is
because we’ve never gotten enough out of Tarrant County to overcome the
margins in rural Texas,” Ms. Davis said of the turnout. “If we don’t get
it to 53 or 54 percent this November, it’s game over. James and Gina can’t
win.” But the state’s Republicans have reasons of their own to be fretful.
Partly because of the recruitment efforts of the Texas Majority PAC and
Blueprint Texas, a down-ballot candidate support organization co-founded
by Ms. Davis earlier this year, the Democrats are fielding a full slate in
all 150 state races for the first time in a half-century. Though many of
these aspirants face long odds, their presence on the ballot could
energize the Democrats in predominantly conservative regions who have not
bothered to turn out in the past. “If we win on Nov. 3, most of those
names running down-ballot in really tough areas like East Texas and the
Hill Country and the Panhandle will be responsible,” Mr. O’Rourke said.
Mr. Henson added that while he remained skeptical about Democratic
enthusiasm being sufficient to carry the day for Mr. Talarico, he also
doubted that a last-minute avalanche of negative ads would prove decisive

James Talarico [ ]CONTRIBUTE [ ]'New York Times: In Texas, Talarico Inspires a Recurring Blue-Tinted Dream In the go-big-or-go-home collective consciousness of Texas, no ambition is deemed too reckless, no daydream too wild. Save perhaps one. It is the idea, fantastical to many as it is irresistible to others, that the Democrats will win a statewide race in Texas for the first time in 32 years. According to the latest New York Times/Siena University poll of the race for U.S. Senate, James Talarico, a 37-year-old state legislator seen by national Democrats as one of the breakout stars of this cycle, is ahead of his Republican rival, Ken Paxton, the state’s scandal-plagued attorney general, by six points. The poll was conducted from Sept. 21 to Sept. 30. A survey from mid-September, the ReconMR/Siena Research Institute poll, also showed the Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Gina Hinojosa, four points ahead of the three-term G.O.P. incumbent, Greg Abbott, the most dominant political figure in Texas. Cue the fluttering heartbeats. Cue, as well, the eye-rolls. Given how thoroughly Republicans have dominated the state, and how the hopes of Democrats have repeatedly crashed, some Texas pollsters remain skeptical. “At some point, you do get conditioned by all that’s happened in the past,” said James Henson, the director of the University of Texas at Austin’s Texas Politics Project. “I mean, you look at the trends and you have to admit that something’s going on. But you still don’t want to believe your lying eyes, because you’ve been burned for so long.” Mr. Henson was referring to the perennial spectacle of much-ballyhooed Texas Democratic aspirants face-planting against the Lone Star State’s red wall. First came Tony Sanchez Jr., the swaggering and self-funding Laredo oilman whom Gov. Rick Perry dispatched in 2002 by an 18-point margin. Next was the state senator Wendy Davis, who attracted worldwide attention for her filibuster in the Texas Legislature against an anti-abortion measure but whom Mr. Abbott demolished by 20 points in 2014. Finally, the El Paso congressman Beto O’Rourke came up 2.6 points short of defeating Senator Ted Cruz in 2018 but then suffered a 10-point loss to Mr. Abbott four years later. Even with the awareness of such humiliations, Democrats find themselves maintaining that 2026 could, at long last, be the year. President Trump’s deep unpopularity and the prospect of a blue wave could, they insist, extend into the state he won by nearly 14 points in 2024. According to a September survey conducted by Texas Southern University, Mr. Trump is seven points underwater in Texas. Mr. Talarico has run an energetic and well-financed campaign, while Mr. Paxton has staged far fewer public events and has had to rely on outside groups to fund an attack-ad blitzkrieg against his Democratic opponent. Mr. Abbott, meanwhile, has outspent Ms. Hinojosa by a 10-to-one ratio, yet has been unable to build an insurmountable lead. “People have vastly underestimated Gina,” said Ms. Davis, now a political consultant and a senior adviser to Planned Parenthood Texas Votes, an advocacy organization. “Dollar for dollar, she’s running the best statewide campaign we’ve ever seen.” Such optimism stands in defiance of the political axiom that Texas is where idealistic Democrats go to be mugged by reality. The party’s demise there is not a product of ill fortune, Mr. Henson said. “Governor Abbott has built an impressive election machine that has benefited state-level Republicans again and again for a decade and a half,” he said. “And the Democratic machinery here is almost nonexistent.” A ‘Hollowing-Out’ I have written about the politics of my native state at regular intervals for more than three decades. After watching the Democrats’ century-long rule in Texas come to a decisive end with Gov. Ann Richards’s loss to George W. Bush in 1994, I saw the party descend into atrophy in which failure begot more failure. “The 30-year drought has done a lot of things,” said Luke Warford, the chairman of the Travis County Democratic Party and the founder of the Agave Democratic Infrastructure Fund. “It’s kept donors on the sidelines, which makes a lot of potentially good candidates not run because there’s no belief they can win. And it also makes a lot of really talented staff leave to find better-paying work in true battleground states.” The Democratic Party has no counterpart to Mr. Abbott, and hasn’t since 1993, when Senator Lloyd Bentsen moved to Washington to join President Bill Clinton’s cabinet. Its weaknesses are even more glaring farther down the hierarchy. In recent elections, as many as one-third of state races have gone uncontested by Democrats. One-fifth of the party’s county chairs and two-thirds of its precinct chairs have been left unfilled. Until last year, the state party had a negative operating budget. As the veteran Democratic consultant Matt Angle observed, “There’s been a hollowing-out of the party.” Still, those of us who recall the satisfied sense of invincibility among Texas Democrats after roughly a century of one-party rule have detected similar signs of overconfidence among the state’s ruling party. The party’s rightward tilt, increasingly forceful with each legislative session, reached its apotheosis in March, with Mr. Paxton’s primary victory over the more moderate Republican four-term incumbent, Senator John Cornyn. Mr. Paxton, a close ally of Mr. Trump’s, was impeached by the Republican-controlled State House (and later acquitted by the State Senate) in 2023 over allegations that included bribery. He was also accused by his wife of adultery. Mr. Trump endorsed him anyway, all but guaranteeing his landslide primary triumph over Mr. Cornyn but in the process testing the allegiance of center-right Texans. In similar fashion, the Texas G.O.P. is in danger of losing many Latino voters who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 after years of siding with Democrats. “We adopted a lazy way of campaigning that bit us on the ass, and we’ve learned from that,” Mr. O’Rourke said. “Now it’s the Republicans who’ve gotten really lazy and complacent and comfortable.” Signs of Republican Overreach Simply spending one week driving through the vastness of Texas, as I did in September, is all it takes to appreciate an underdog party’s uphill battle. The state’s 32 million residents are spread across 20 media markets, many of them distinct ecosystems, from the urban colossi of Houston and the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex to the oil patch of the Texas Panhandle to the Latino-dominated borderlands of the Rio Grande Valley. “When national donors are deciding where to invest, they look at a place like Iowa, where $5 million can fully fund a race,” said Katherine Fischer, the director of the Texas Majority PAC, which was established by the liberal philanthropist Soros family. “That’s why Texas is always at the bottom of their list. It’s just so damned big.” Reaching so many markets presents a daunting challenge for an upstart candidate like Ms. Hinojosa, a state representative from the border city of Brownsville. “There’s still 20 percent of the electorate that doesn’t know who I am,” she said in an interview in mid-September. To date, Ms. Hinojosa’s campaign has said that it has raised about $20 million. For his part, Mr. Talarico spent about $30 million earlier this year to introduce himself statewide as a man of Christian faith and a member of the Texas House with a record of supporting bipartisan legislation. Since that time, however, Mr. Paxton and his associates have invested more than $100 million in an effort to redefine his opponent as “radical” and “weird,” with ads that quote from remarks Mr. Talarico made several years ago (and later renounced) suggesting that “God is nonbinary” and that there are six biological sexes. Mr. Paxton and his allies have at times questioned Mr. Talarico’s manhood and even his Christianity, an effort to jolt the sensibilities of a state prone to mythologizing godly and masculine archetypes. “How they’re negatively defining Talarico is kind of a bank-shot way of saying that he’s not a true Texas conservative,” Mr. Henson said. Whether money can overwhelm conditions on the ground is the riddle looming over the Texas races. In the border city of Laredo, which Mr. Trump won in 2024 — the first time a Republican had done so in over a century — signs of buyer’s remorse are evident. Arrests by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in Laredo were higher in July than in any other American city. Mr. Trump’s erratic trade policies have further created instability at the city’s port of entry. While acknowledging the economic concerns that many border residents share, Adrian Zapata, a business executive in the health industry who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, said in an interview that the negative ads against Mr. Talarico were resonating with some of his family members. “They see Talarico as an ultraliberal,” he said. “They’re done with the ‘they/them.’ They’re going to vote for Paxton just because of that.” As for Mr. Zapata, “I’m not ready to vote for Talarico,” he said. “But I don’t like Paxton. He’s never done anything for South Texas, and his personal and business dealings have hurt him a lot with folks down here.” There is a similarly muddled electoral picture in the cattle country of deep West Texas adjacent to Big Bend National Park. Mr. Trump and Mr. Abbott have aggressively championed a border wall and artificial intelligence data centers, both of which threaten to disrupt the region’s pastoral ethos. A coalition of more than 200 landowners has sued the federal government over the border wall, while other residents have circulated a petition to protest the construction of a new data center near Fort Stockton. George Johnson, a cattle feed operator in Alpine, waved off such concerns, saying: “Folks worrying about data centers were also worried when the internet got started. It’s Talarico who scares me to death, him and all that socialist talk.” Others in this largely conservative region harbor the view that Republicans have failed to make good on their promises. Thaddeus Cleveland, the Republican sheriff of Terrell County, said that both he and his county had voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, but added, “Everything he campaigned on, we’re seeing the opposite of, like going to war.” Sheriff Cleveland predicted that the negative campaign ads by the Republicans would not factor as significantly into the votes of his neighbors as “the price of groceries and gas, which are compounded here because we’re so far from everywhere else.” But it is in purple Tarrant County, dominated by Fort Worth, where the party could pay the price for having potentially overestimated its mandate from the voters. Conservative leaders have cut funds for nonprofits that aid at-risk children, subjected school library books to right-wing litmus tests and eliminated free bus rides to polling stations in poor neighborhoods. “The far-right leaders here have implemented Project 2025 on a county level,” said Alisa Simmons, a Democrat and county commissioner who is running to unseat the conservative county judge, Tim O’Hare. In an early sign this year that area Republicans may be out of step with Tarrant County’s constituents, a Democratic aviation machinist and union leader, Taylor Rehmet, defeated Leigh Wambsganss, a well-funded Republican Christian activist who led the conservative takeover of several metroplex school boards. He won by 14 points in a January special election for a State Senate seat covering a region that Mr. Trump won by 17 points in 2024. A ‘Gradualist’ Theory Which party prevails in Texas is a complicated riddle. Historically a low-turnout state — it ranked second to last in the 2024 election, ahead of only Arkansas — Texas held a primary in March that saw nearly one in four voters showing up to the polls, a modern record for midterm participation, with Democrats slightly outpacing Republicans. A few factors could conspire to thwart a blue wave in Texas. As of 2020, straight-ticket voting is no longer possible in the state, which could impact the mostly Democratic urban counties where that practice has frequently been used by voters in past elections. Texas is one of only eight states that lack universal online registration, while voting by mail is also highly restricted. In January, Mr. Abbott turned over the state’s list of approximately 18.7 million registered voters to the Trump administration, and 1.2 million of them have subsequently been put on the “suspense list” because their addresses have not been verified. The recent shuttering of nearly one-third of Tarrant County’s polling sites by its Republican-controlled county commission is particularly worrisome for Democrats. “The reason we’ve lost these statewide races in the past is because we’ve never gotten enough out of Tarrant County to overcome the margins in rural Texas,” Ms. Davis said of the turnout. “If we don’t get it to 53 or 54 percent this November, it’s game over. James and Gina can’t win.” But the state’s Republicans have reasons of their own to be fretful. Partly because of the recruitment efforts of the Texas Majority PAC and Blueprint Texas, a down-ballot candidate support organization co-founded by Ms. Davis earlier this year, the Democrats are fielding a full slate in all 150 state races for the first time in a half-century. Though many of these aspirants face long odds, their presence on the ballot could energize the Democrats in predominantly conservative regions who have not bothered to turn out in the past. “If we win on Nov. 3, most of those names running down-ballot in really tough areas like East Texas and the Hill Country and the Panhandle will be responsible,” Mr. O’Rourke said. name: Melat Kiros
subject: 3 Days Left: These Evil Ballot Measures Might Pass
body:
Trans rights are hanging in the balance
| |
---
| Peter, I know we have been calling and texting you, relentlessly asking you all to get back on the doors and talk to your neighbors. I want to be extremely clear: We aren’t doing this work just to get me to Congress, **we’re doing this to advance human rights and progressive politics up and down the ballot.** [If we want to tax the rich, and reject the billionaire ballot measures around the state, we need more canvassers to sign up for the final 3 days of this election.](https://www.solidarity.tech/ahoy/messages/jT91oBMQrPxru9korvjV92BoGrtqHci6/click?signature=01fa2b834b31de10f6c01fcaed2f1fb3195c0c9d&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwin.kirosforco.com%2F) Real talk: **Recent polling came out that has prop 134 and 135 tied for whether or not they pass.** Trans rights are hanging in the balance and that’s why I am sending this message now. **Here are some things you can do to protect trans rights, lock in to help us win big, and tax the rich:**
1. [**Canvass:** ](https://www.solidarity.tech/ahoy/messages/jT91oBMQrPxru9korvjV92BoGrtqHci6/click?signature=01fa2b834b31de10f6c01fcaed2f1fb3195c0c9d&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwin.kirosforco.com%2F)Sign up to talk to your neighbors, in person, about the ballot measures and why they matter. We set a goal of talking to 20,000 of our neighbors this month and we can only hit that goal if we have enough people like you.
2. [**Phonebank:** ](https://www.solidarity.tech/ahoy/messages/jT91oBMQrPxru9korvjV92BoGrtqHci6/click?signature=ac3b64b092d86a6d5b0e3741815f0450bbeeadb9&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.mobilize.us%2Ffamiliesnotpolitics%2F)Our partners at no slate are calling people around the state all day, every day, to get the word out about the ballot for all coloradans

**Bonus: Invite your friends to all of the above!!!** If you aren't into organized fun and prefer to help on your own time, a website has been created to support our trans neighbors and get more ballots in. At any time, you can head to [www.defendourneighbors.com](https://www.solidarity.tech/ahoy/messages/jT91oBMQrPxru9korvjV92BoGrtqHci6/click?signature=ee9f5e5d0e9e1a2dca7a2a25a4be9caa9f8ea37f&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.defendourneighbors.com) (Defend Our Neighbors) to canvass people nearby, find your neighbors that haven’t turned in their ballot, and remind them to vote! [Let’s win big and run these billionaires out of Colorado.](https://www.solidarity.tech/ahoy/messages/jT91oBMQrPxru9korvjV92BoGrtqHci6/click?signature=01fa2b834b31de10f6c01fcaed2f1fb3195c0c9d&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwin.kirosforco.com%2F) See you out there! Melat

name: Wes Moore
subject: One of the final requests
body:
# [](https://act.wesmoore.com/go/8?t=1&akid=2253%2E1086043%2E9ryWsj)
Peter,
In a moment, I’m going to make one of my final requests of you before the end of our re-election campaign:
**[I’m asking you to make your first donation* before Election Day. We’re in the final hours of this campaign, so even $1 would have an impact.](https://act.wesmoore.com/go/417?c0=wes-em-20261101-4.SZuKTb&refcode=em-20261101-4&t=3&akid=2253%2E1086043%2E9ryWsj)**
Please, let me explain why I’m asking you for one of the last times.
The polls will close in just two days. We’re finalizing our plans for the last push to get out the vote on Election Day so every eligible Marylander gets to the polls and we can win this thing.
But what we do in these final hours matters. Dan Cox and the MAGA Republicans supporting him have been on the attack, and they’re ready to do whatever they can to stop us from winning this race.
I’m so grateful that you read these messages from me and stay updated with our re-election campaign. This grassroots team is the reason why we will win. Hey folks,
This one is genuinely disturbing.
Pete Hegseth has fired another senior Army general, Laura Loomer is taking a victory lap, and Donald Trump is publicly threatening a decorated military officer he doesn't even seem to know. We're watching serious questions emerge about who's influencing decisions at the Pentagon--and what happens when political loyalty starts taking priority over national security.
Here's what we cover:
* [**00:00:18**] Trump threatens Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia on camera--and gets basic facts about him wrong.
* [**00:02:40**] I explain my own history with Laura Loomer and why her apparent influence over the Trump administration is so alarming.
* [**00:04:27**] Loomer celebrates Sylvia's firing as questions emerge about information allegedly shared with her by Pentagon officials.
* [**00:06:21**] We break down the accusations against Sylvia, the unanswered questions, and the possibility of political loyalty tests inside the military.
* [**00:09:36**] A bizarre series of freezer failures at military bases raises another set of questions about Pentagon security and leadership.

This isn't just about one general losing his job. It's about the people making decisions that affect our troops, our national security, and the country we all share. We dig into the allegations, the political pressure, and the growing concerns about Hegseth's leadership. Your generosity and your personal investment in this grassroots movement allowed us to accomplish all of these things and more throughout this campaign: [](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/142684639/657701020/-147829035?refcode=ea.54c65ead-15d6-f111-bf5b-000d3a54442e&ms=ea.54c65ead-15d6-f111-bf5b-000d3a54442e&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMTAvMS84MTM2MiIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICI1NGM2NWVhZC0xNWQ2LWYxMTEtYmY1Yi0wMDBkM2E1NDQ0MmUiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=RosKSbfSfZoJY7uyced7qPMOkNmndLx091vFOdBZkKk=) Right now, I'd like to set our collective sights on our next challenge: getting out every single vote we can until Election Day. **Because complacency is one of our biggest opponents in this race. And the job's not done until the polls close.** I am ready to hit the ground running on day one as your next governor, and get to work on the policy plans we've made together. I am ready to _fight like hell_ for freedom, affordability, and opportunity. And I am ready to stand up to bullies everywhere — even in the Trump administration — when they try to harm the people of our state. That's the kind of governor I'll be. _However, none of those things can take place if we don't give it our all in these final days._ So right until the moment the polls close, let's talk to neighbors. ## Menlo Park Measure P isn’t about Housing, it’s about Local Control
---
Peter Ohtaki — October 6, 2026
---
The State of California is coming after our parking plazas. Like Menlo Park, most Peninsula cities have parking plazas behind your main street merchants – Laurel St in San Carlos, Santa Cruz Ave in Los Gatos, Main St in Los Altos, Castro St in Mountain View, California Ave in Palo Alto, and Burlingame Ave. Sacramento wants Menlo Park to build 600 housing units on the parking plazas that enable mid-Peninsula customers to shop at our downtown merchants and restaurants.
---
Don’t be misled by signs saying Menlo Park isn’t building enough housing. 3,480 apartments are going through the city’s approval process, which exceeds the 2,946 units required under the city’s Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA), and will increase our housing stock by 20% - at least 7,200 new residents.
---
|
---
Meta has laid off thousands of employees, and a half million have moved from California. Yet the politicians in Sacramento continue to force unrealistic regional housing needs allocations to the cities with no state funding for the infrastructure and classrooms needed – an unfunded state mandate, requiring the cities to pick up the tab. Before we give up our downtown parking plazas, Menlo Park residents want a say – vote Yes on P to give residents a voice in the future of our downtown. Don’t let Sacramento take away local control!
#### **Vote Yes on Measure P**
[**_Save Downtown Menlo_**](https://g3j1.engage.squarespace-mail.com/r?m=6ae7705b328dc46ada867428&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.savedowntownmenlo.org%2F&w=6619ff0a31aa07375378c596&c=b_6ae6eac84aab1455ef11c91a&l=en-US&s=N9pArGwahHZ6P_UxWopZIlb9F_Y%3D), a grassroots coalition of residents and business owners, is fighting back with a **ballot measure** that would require **voter approval** before any downtown parking lots can be repurposed. **If you are a Menlo Park voter, on November 3rd** vote for the initiative! **Don’t sacrifice our downtown** Let’s utilized [Alternate Sites](https://g3j1.engage.squarespace-mail.com/r?m=6ae7705b328dc46ada867428&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.savedowntownmenlo.org%2Falternativesites&w=6619ff0a31aa07375378c596&c=b_6ae6eac84aab1455ef11c91a&l=en-US&s=2AqZARvYi596YWwjY07cas4ytyE%3D) BEFORE irrevocably changing our charming Menlo Park downtown.
---
|
---
| Once the parking lots are gone, our welcoming downtown character will be GONE.
---
**Stand up for local control and common sense**. If we lose Downtown Menlo Park, what comes next? **_Your Peninsula city may be next for your downtown parking lots!_** ✅ [**_Donate here_**](https://g3j1.engage.squarespace-mail.com/r?m=6ae7705b328dc46ada867428&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.efundraisingconnections.com%2Fc%2FSAVEDOWNTOWNMENLO&w=6619ff0a31aa07375378c596&c=b_6ae6eac84aab1455ef11c91a&l=en-US&s=w_INJdXASWzhZkIqnAk0wsNwgaQ%3D) to support the campaign
✅ **Forward this email to your friends in Menlo Park!**
